turns.text: Who is the jnani? The witness or the supreme?
And what about the person? What comes first, the person or the knower?
The jnani is the supreme and also the witness. He is both being and awareness. In relation to consciousness he is awareness. In relation to the universe he is pure being.

The person is a very small thing. Actually it is a composite, it cannot be said to exist by itself. Unperceived, it is just not there. It is but the shadow of the mind, the sum total of memories. Pure being is reflected in the mirror of the mind, as knowing. What is known takes the shape of a person, based on memory and habit.
All desires are painful, the holy as well as the unholy.
Are you living in the Supreme Unknown?
What makes you say so?
And if I desire nothing, not even the Supreme?
They are not the same and pain is not the same. Passion is painful, compassion -- never. The entire universe strives to fulfil a desire born of compassion.
Where else?
No desire ever arises in my mind.
Then you are as good as dead, or you are the Supreme.
What is your work?
I am a probation officer.
Who works? Work happens to take place.
I need it for the sake of money. I like it, because it puts me in touch with living beings.
They may need me and it is their destinies that made me take up this work. It is one life, after all.
Must you work?
Do you need to work?
What do you need them for?
You say that nothing happens to you. Are you not affected at all by the suffering in the world?
But you see it. Does seeing not make you responsible?
So you feel nothing when people suffer?
Is it not cruel to stand apart like that?
Suffering happens in consciousness, like clouds passing in the sky. I am not the cloud, I am the space in which it appears.
Seeing clearly is compassion. To suffer because others suffer is still ignorance. In clear seeing, right action happens by itself.
There is feeling, but no owner of feeling. Pain is there, but not the story 'this should not be'. The story is your personal addition.
Cruelty is to remain confused and add your fear and anger to the world. Wake up from the dream of being a separate sufferer; only then can your presence be truly helpful.
However much I listen to you, the fear of death does not leave me.
It feels like I, as this person, will vanish and that terrifies me.
But deep sleep comes and goes. Death seems final.
How can I be sure I am this screen and not the story?
Who is afraid? The body, which is going to end anyway, or the witness, which never began?
Every night in deep sleep this person vanishes, yet you are not terrified then. You enjoy the rest. Only waking imagination calls it death and trembles.
Final for whom? The forms change, the movie ends, but the screen remains unstained. Find yourself as the screen, not the story.
Right now, notice that all that appears — body, thoughts, fear of death — is known. The knower is not in danger. Attend to the knower, not to what it knows.
Sometimes you say effort is needed, sometimes you say all is grace. Which is true?
If all is grace, why bother to make any effort at all?
I still feel I must do something to deserve realisation.
So should I strive or surrender?
Effort belongs to the person, grace to reality. Your effort prepares the ground; grace is the rain. Both are needed for the crop.
The impulse to 'bother' or not is itself grace. Even your laziness is seen. That which sees is not lazy. Stay with that.
Deserving is a childish idea. Your only 'doing' is to stop pretending you are what you are not. Grace is already there as your very being.
Strive until striving exhausts itself and surrender happens by itself. Both are movements in the same one consciousness that you are.
My Guru gave me a mantra. You tell me to stay with 'I am'. Should I drop the mantra?
The mantra calms me, but sometimes I just repeat it mechanically.
So is 'I am' also a mantra?
If I let go of all words, I feel lost.
If a boat has brought you to the other shore, you do not carry it on your head. Use what helps you to be still and present; discard what keeps you busy and dull.
Mechanical repetition puts the body to sleep and leaves the mind dreaming. Let the words point you back to the sense of being, then stay with that nakedly.
'I am' is not a sound to worship but a fact to see. The mantra is a finger; 'I am' is the moon it points to. Look where it points, not at the finger.
You are not lost; your usual distractions are missing. Stay with that bare discomfort; it is the threshold of reality, not a mistake.
I have a family and many responsibilities. Is it not selfish to turn inward and think of freedom?
But my family expects attention and care. Won't they suffer if I withdraw into myself?
Sometimes I feel torn between spiritual practice and practical life.
So I do not need to leave anything?
You are selfish now, because you take yourself to be this one body-mind and seek its security. To discover your real nature is the end of selfishness, not its peak.
You do not have to withdraw from them, only from your fantasies about them. Be fully present, free of anxiety and claims; then your actions will be simple and kind.
Life is your practice. Let every demand, every irritation, every joy throw you back on the question: 'To whom does this come?' Use your family as a mirror, not as a chain.
Leave only your ignorance of yourself. What needs to fall away will fall away by itself, when you stop holding it with fear and habit.
In dream, things seem real, but they vanish on waking. How do I know this waking state is not just a longer dream?
So what should I trust, if not the world I see?
But even 'I am' disappears in deep sleep.
Can this source be experienced?
You do not know. You assume. In both states, there is one constant: the sense 'I am' which witnesses their coming and going.
Trust the fact that you are, not what you appear to be. Appearances contradict each other; the being that knows them does not change.
The memory of 'I am' disappears. The potential to know does not. From that potential, both dream and waking spring. Be interested in the source, not its waves.
Experience needs subject and object. The source is before both. You cannot experience it, but you can cease to pretend you are anything else.
Is there free will, or is everything predetermined?
Then why do I feel I am choosing all the time?
If there is no real choice, what is the point of effort or practice?
So should I act as if I have free will or not?
For the person you take yourself to be, there is neither freedom nor bondage. It is a bundle of tendencies acting itself out. For the reality that you are, the question does not arise.
A leaf moved by the wind may feel it is deciding where to fall. Your feeling of choice is just the mind commenting on movements it does not understand.
Effort appears as part of the play. It refines the mind, makes it transparent. Then it becomes clear that what you really are was never bound by any destiny.
Act as you must, but do not conclude anything from it. Let actions happen, and stay with the silent fact of being in which they rise and set.
This infinite and eternal self of mine, how am I to know it?
How am I to be rid of the mind? And is life without mind at all possible on the human level?
Which ideas are wrong and which are true?
One cannot live by denying everything!
I find being alive a painful state.
All I know is that I do not know myself.
If I am neither the body nor mind, how am I aware of them? How can I perceive something quite foreign to myself?

The self you want to know, is it some second self? Are you made of several selves? Surely, there is only one self and you are that self. The self you are is the only self there is. Remove and abandon your wrong ideas about yourself and there it is, in all its glory. It is only your mind that prevents self-knowledge.
There is no such thing as mind. There are ideas and some of them are wrong. Abandon the wrong ideas, for they are false and obstruct your vision of yourself.
Assertions are usually wrong and denials -- right.

Only by denying can one live. Assertion is bondage. To question and deny is necessary. It is the essence of revolt and without revolt there can be no freedom. There is no second, or higher self to search for. You are the highest self, only give up the false ideas you have about your self. Both faith and reason tell you that you are neither the body, nor its desires and fears, nor are you the mind with its fanciful ideas, nor the role society compels you to play, the person you are supposed to be. Give up the false and the true will come into its own. You say you want to know your self. You are your self -- you cannot be anything but what you are. Is knowing separate from being? Whatever you can know with your mind is of the mind, not you; about yourself you can only say: 'I am, I am aware, I like It'.

You cannot be alive for you are life itself. It is the person you imagine yourself to be that suffers, not you. Dissolve it in awareness. It is merely a bundle of memories and habits. From the awareness of the unreal to the awareness of your real nature there is a chasm which you will easily cross, once you have mastered the art of pure awareness.

How do you know, that you do not know your self? Your direct insight tells you that yourself you know first, for nothing exists to you without your being there to experience its existence. You imagine you do not know your self, because you cannot describe your self. You can always say: 'I know that I am' and you will refuse as untrue the statement: 'I am not'. But whatever can be described cannot be your self, and what you are cannot be described. You can only know your self by being yourself without any attempt at self-definition and self-description. Once you have understood that you are nothing perceivable or conceivable, that whatever appears in the field of consciousness cannot be your self, you will apply yourself to the eradication of all self-identification, as the only way that can take you to a deeper realisation of your self. You literally progress by rejection -- a veritable rocket. To know that you are neither in the body nor in the mind, though aware of both, is already self-knowledge.

'Nothing is me,' is the first step. 'Everything is me' is the next. Both hang on the idea: 'there is a world'. When this too is given up, you remain what you are -- the non-dual Self. You are it here and now, but your vision is obstructed by your false ideas about your self.

All I know is the stream of consciousness, an endless succession of events. The river of time flows, bringing and carrying away relentlessly. Transformation of the future into past is going on all the time.
What does it mean -- time will cease?
But what does it mean in actual experience? How do you know that for you time has ceased?
I can imagine a sort of cosmic memory, accessible with some training. But how can the future be known? The unexpected is inevitable.

Are you not the victim of your language? You speak about the flow of time, as if you were stationary. But the events you have witnessed yesterday somebody else may see tomorrow. It is you who are in movement and not time. Stop moving and time will cease.
Past and future will merge in the eternal now.
It may mean that past and future do not matter any more. It may also mean that all that happened and will happen becomes an open book to be read at will.

What is unexpected on one level may be certain to happen, when seen from a higher level After all, we are within the limits of the mind. In reality nothing happens, there is no past nor future; all appears and nothing is.
What does it mean, nothing is? Do you turn blank, or go to sleep? Or do you dissolve the world and keep us all in abeyance, until we are brought back to life at the next flicker of your thought?
You mean to say an experience can be nameless, formless, undefined?
If it is not conscious, why talk about it?
Can one be aware of the unconscious? How is it done?
Does it mean that the unconscious becomes conscious?
I am puzzled. How can one be aware and yet unconscious?

Oh, no, it is not that bad. The world of mind and matter, of names and shapes, continues, but it does not matter to me at all. It is like having a shadow. It is there -- following me wherever I go, but not hindering me in any way. It remains a world of experiences, but not of names and forms related to me by desires and fears. The experiences are qualityless, pure experiences, if I may say so. I call them experiences for the lack of a better word. They are like the waves on the surface of the ocean, the ever-present, but not affecting its peaceful power.

In the beginning all experience is such. It is only desire and fear, born of memory, that give it name and form and separate it from other experiences. It is not a conscious experience, for it is not in opposition to other experiences, yet it is an experience all the same.
Most of your experiences are unconscious. The conscious ones are very few. You are unaware of the fact because to you only the conscious ones count. Become aware of the unconscious .
Desire and fear are the obscuring and distorting factors. When mind is free of them the unconscious becomes accessible.
It is rather the other way round. The conscious becomes one with the unconscious. The distinction ceases, whichever way you look at it.

Awareness is not limited to consciousness. It is of all that is. Consciousness is of duality. There is no duality in awareness. It is one single block of pure cognition. In the same way one can talk of the pure being and pure creation -- nameless, formless, silent and yet absolutely real, powerful, effective. Their being indescribable does not affect them in the least. While they are unconscious, they are essential. The conscious cannot change fundamentally, it can only modify. Any thing, to change, must pass through death, through obscuration and dissolution. Gold jewellery must be melted down before it is cast into another shape. What refuses to die cannot be reborn.

My question remains unanswered. You are merely describing what I know -- life and its sorrows. But who is responsible, you do not say. When I press you, you throw the blame on God, or karma, or on my own greed and fear -- which merely invites further questions. Give me the final answer.

I am asking about the immediate, the transitory, the appearance. Here is a picture of a child killed by soldiers. It is a fact -- staring at you. You cannot deny it. Now, who is responsible for the death of the child?
Your people speak of karma and retribution.
So, the innocent suffers for the guilty?
The final answer is this: nothing is. All is a momentary appearance in the field of the universal consciousness; continuity as name and form is a mental formation only, easy to dispel.

Nobody and everybody. The world is what it contains and each thing affects all others. We all kill the child and we all die with it. Every event has innumerable causes and produces numberless effects. It is useless to keep accounts, nothing is traceable.
It is merely a gross approximation: in reality we are all creators and creatures of each other, causing and bearing each other's burden.

In our ignorance we are innocent; in our actions we are guilty. We sin without knowing and suffer without understanding. Our only hope: to stop, to look, to understand and to get out of the traps of memory. For memory feeds imagination and imagination generates desire and fear.
Does this knowledge come to you from within or from outside?
I cannot grasp how inner can be outer.
Still, I feel knowledge must come from somewhere.
So knowledge is not really transmitted?
It does not apply. My inner is outside and my outer is inside. I may get from you the knowledge needed at the moment, but you are not apart from me.
You take space and distance as real. In truth there is no distance. Things are as you see them; when you see rightly, you find the separation was imagined.
Knowledge appears where understanding is ripe. What is called 'from within' and 'from without' is only the mind drawing divisions.
It appears as needed, like a reflection in a mirror. The mirror does not send or receive. It merely shows.
What is "turiya"?
Then these names describe distinct states?
Then why use them at all?
Is naming always misleading?
To be the point of light tracing the world is turiya. To be the light itself is turiyatita.
They describe the mind’s attempt to mark what cannot be marked. Names arise from the need to communicate, not from the reality they try to point to.
Because you ask. But having answered, I show you the limitation: reality is so near that naming it pushes it away.
It is useful until it becomes a cage. Use the name to turn inward, then drop even the turning.
Is there progress? Or growth? Does your vision expand with time?
How do the gunas affect spiritual life?
Can one overcome them?
So even stagnation can be useful?
Then what is my responsibility?
Reality does not grow. It is unmoving. What you call progress is the play of the gunas.
Sattva clarifies, rajas distracts, tamas obscures. Together they weave the sense of becoming.
You overcome them by seeing them. The moment you recognise tamas in yourself, it loses its hold.
It shows you your attachments. The guna does not bind you; your clinging to its movement binds you.
To see clearly. To act when appropriate. To refrain when not. The gunas will continue to play, but you need not be their puppet.
A grain of sand is a thing. A planet is a thing. How are these related to consciousness?
Do you mean things are outside consciousness?
Then what is the foundation of the physical world?
This is difficult to accept.
Where consciousness does not reach, matter begins.
A 'thing' is only a form of being you have not understood. When you understand, you will see no things — only consciousness taking shapes.
Memory. The world persists because memory repeats patterns. When memory ceases, the world dissolves like a dream upon waking.
It is difficult because you take your concepts as facts. See concepts as concepts, and the world becomes transparent.
Is there no escape from all this?
Where is it? I do not see it.
If I am the One, why do I feel trapped?
How does one cease?
I am doing nothing else but showing the escape.
Understand that the One includes the Three — creation, preservation, destruction. You are the One, not the movement.
Because you identify with the movement. A wave cannot escape the ocean until it ceases to be only a wave.
By giving up identification. When self-identification is abandoned, what you are remains by itself — free.
I must select my Guru rightly.
You are not answering my question: how to find the right Guru?
By his grace I shall be made happy, powerful and peaceful.
I know only my conditioned existence; there is nothing else.
I know nothing of it.
I see your point. While awake, I know that I am, but am not happy; in sleep I am, I am happy, but I do not know it. All I need is to know that I am free and happy.
All this I grasp verbally, but it does not become a part of myself. It remains as a picture in my mind to be looked at. Is it not the task of the Guru to give life to the picture?
Be the right man and the right Guru will surely find you.

But I did answer your question. Do not look for a Guru, do not even think of one. Make your goal your Guru. After all, the Guru is but a means to an end, not the end in itself. He is not important, it is what you expect of him that matters to you. Now, what do you expect?

What ambitions! How can a person limited in time and space, a mere body-mind, a gasp of pain between birth and death, be happy? The very conditions of its arising make happiness impossible. Peace, power, happiness, these are never personal states, nobody can say 'my peace', 'my power' -- because 'mine' implies exclusivity, which is fragile and insecure.
Surely, you cannot say so. In deep sleep you are not conditioned. How ready and willing you are to go to sleep, how peaceful, free and happy you are when asleep!
Put it negatively. When you sleep, you are not in pain, nor bound, nor restless.

Quite so. Now, go within, into a state which you may compare to a state of waking sleep, in which you are aware of yourself, but not of the world. In that state you will know, without the least trace of doubt, that at the root of your being you are free and happy. The only trouble is that you are addicted to experience and you cherish your memories. In reality it is the other way round; what is remembered is never real; the real is now.

Again, it is the other way round. The picture is alive; dead is the mind. As the mind is made of words and images, so is every reflection in the mind. It covers up reality with verbalisation and then complains. You say a Guru is needed, to do miracles with you. You are playing with words only. The Guru and the disciple are one single thing, like the candle and its flame. Unless the disciple is earnest, he cannot be called a disciple. Unless a Guru is all love and self-giving, he cannot be called a Guru. Only reality begets reality, not the false.
I can see that I am false. Who will make me true?

I do not grasp you fully. On one hand you say a Guru is needed; on the other -- the Guru can only give advice, but the effort is mine. Please state clearly -- can one realise the Self without a Guru, or is the finding of a true Guru essential?
I have a Guru and I love him very much. But whether he is my true Guru I do not know.
When I meet a European with some education and talk to him about a Guru and his teachings, his reaction is: 'the man must be mad to teach such nonsense'. What am I to tell him?
How strange! I cannot imagine life without a Guru.
This constant repetition of a few words, is it not a kind of madness?

The very words you said will do it. The sentence: 'I can see that I am false' contains all you need for liberation. Ponder over it, go into it deeply, go to the root of it; it will operate. The power is in the word, not in the person.

More essential is the finding of a true disciple. Believe me, a true disciple is very rare, for in no time he goes beyond the need for a Guru, by finding his own self. Do not waste your time on trying to make out whether the advice you get flows from knowledge only, or from valid experience! Just follow it faithfully. Life will bring you another Guru, if another one is needed. Or deprive you of all outer guidance and leave you to your own lights. It is very important to understand that it is the teaching that matters, not the person or the Guru. You get a letter that makes you laugh or cry. It is not the postman who does it. The Guru only tells you the good news about your real Self and shows you the way back to it. In a way the Guru is its messenger. There will be many messengers, but the message is one: be what you are. Or, you can put it differently: Until you realise yourself, you cannot know who is your real Guru. When you realise, you find that all the Gurus you had have contributed to your awakening. Your realisation is the proof that your Guru was real. Therefore, take him as he is, do what he tells you, with earnestness and zeal and trust your heart to warn you if anything goes wrong. If doubt sets in, do not fight it. Cling to what is doubtless and leave the doubtful alone.

Watch yourself. If you see yourself changing, growing, it means you have found the right man. He may be beautiful or ugly, pleasant or unpleasant, flattering you or scolding; nothing matters except the one crucial fact of inward growth. If you do not, well, he may be your friend, but not your Guru.

Take him to himself. Show him, how little he knows himself, how he takes the most absurd statements about himself for holy truth. He is told that he is the body, was born, will die, has parents, duties, learns to like what others like and fear what others fear. Totally a creature of heredity and society, he lives by memory and acts by habits. Ignorant of himself and his true interests, he pursues false aims and is always frustrated. His life and death are meaningless and painful, and there seems to be no way out. Then tell him, there is a way out within his easy reach, not a conversion to another set of ideas, but a liberation from all ideas and patterns of living. Do not tell him about Gurus and disciples -- this way of thinking is not for him. His is an inner path, he is moved by an inner urge and guided by an inner light. Invite him to rebel and he will respond. Do not try to impress on him that so-and-so is a realised man and can be accepted as a Guru. As long as he does not trust himself, he cannot trust another. And confidence will come with experience.
It is a matter of temperament. You too are right. For you, singing the praises of God is enough. You need not desire realisation or take up a sadhana. God's name is all the food you need. Live on it.

It is madness, but it is a deliberate madness. All repetitiveness is tamas, but repeating the name of God is sattva-tamas due to its high purpose. Because of the presence of sattva, the tamas will wear out and will take the shape of complete dispassion, detachment, relinquishment, aloofness, immutability. Tamas becomes the firm foundation on which an integrated life can be lived. The immutable neither lives nor dies; it is the timeless witness of life and death.
My case is hopeless.
You are telling me to live by memory?

Many Gurus have the habit of giving tokens of their grace -- their head cloth, or their sticks, or begging bowl, or robe, thus transmitting or confirming the self-realisation of their disciples. I can see no value in such practices. It is not self-realisation that is transmitted, but self-importance. Of what earthly use is being told something very flattering, but not true? On one hand you are warning me against the many self-styled Gurus, on the other you want me to trust you. Why do you claim to be an exception?
It seems too good to be true.
Have I not suffered enough?
Whatever may be the cause; I am dull. I have neither the will nor the energy.
Is it right to change Gurus?

In a way yours is a most hopeful case. There is an alternative to sadhana, which is trust. If you cannot have the conviction born from fruitful search, then take advantage of my discovery, which I am so eager to share with you. I can see with the utmost clarity that you have never been, nor are, nor will be estranged from reality, that you are the fullness of perfection here and now and that nothing can deprive you of your heritage, of what you are. You are in no way different from me, only you do not know it. You do not know what you are and therefore you imagine your self to be what you are not. Hence desires and fear and overwhelming despair. And meaningless activity in order to escape. Just trust me and live by trusting me. I shall not mislead you. You are the Supreme Reality beyond the world and its creator, beyond consciousness and its witness, beyond all assertions and denials. Remember it, think of it, act on it. Abandon all sense of separation, see yourself in all and act accordingly. With action bliss will come and, with bliss, conviction. After all, you doubt yourself because you are in sorrow. Happiness, natural, spontaneous and lasting cannot be imagined. Either it is there, or it is not. Once you begin to experience the peace, love and happiness which need no outer causes, all your doubts will dissolve. Just catch hold of what I told you and live by it.

You are living by memory anyhow. I am merely asking you to replace the old memories by the memory of what I told you. As you were acting on your old memories, act on the new one. Do not be afraid. For some time there is bound to be a conflict between the old and the new, but if you put yourself resolutely on the side of the new, the strife will soon come to an end and you will realise the effortless state of being oneself, of not being deceived by desires and fears born of illusion.

I do not ask you to trust me. Trust my words and remember them, I want your happiness, not mine. Distrust those who put a distance between you and your true being and offer themselves as a go-between. I do nothing of the kind. I do not even make any promises. I merely say: if you trust my words and put them to test, you will for yourself discover how absolutely true they are. If you ask for a proof before you venture, I can only say: I am the proof. I did trust my teacher's words and kept them in my mind and I did find that he was right, that I was, am and shall be the Infinite Reality, embracing all, transcending all. As you say, you have neither the time nor the energy for lengthy practices. I offer you an alternative. Accept my words on trust and live anew, or live and die in sorrow.

Do not be misled by the simplicity of the advice. Very few are those who have the courage to trust the innocent and the simple. To know that you are a prisoner of your mind, that you live in an imaginary world of your own creation is the dawn of wisdom. To want nothing of it, to be ready to abandon it entirely, is earnestness. Only such earnestness, born of true despair, will make you trust me.

Suffering has made you dull, unable to see its enormity. Your first task is to see the sorrow in you and around you; your next to long intensely for liberation. The very intensity of longing will guide you; you need no other guide.
Oh, no. You have enough for the first step. And each step will generate enough energy for the next. Energy comes with confidence and confidence comes with experience.

Why not change? Gurus are like milestones? It is natural to move on from one to another. Each tells you the direction and the distance, while the sadguru, the eternal Guru, is the road itself. Once you realise that the road is the goal and that you are always on the road, not to reach a goal, but to enjoy its beauty and its wisdom, life ceases to be a task and becomes natural and simple, in itself an ecstasy.
What is the cause of desire and fear?
How to put an end to memory?

You maintain that without me there would be no world, and that the world and my knowledge of the world are identical. Science has come to a quite different conclusion: the world exists as something concrete and continuous, while I am a by-product of biological evolution of the nervous system, which is primarily not so much a seat of consciousness, as a mechanism of survival as individual and species. Yours is altogether a subjective view, while science tries to describe everything in objective terms. Is this contradiction inevitable?
But what is true? What comes first, mind or matter?
Obviously, the memory of past pains and pleasures. There is no great mystery about it. Conflict arises only when desire and fear refer to the same object.

It is neither necessary, nor possible. realise that all happens in consciousness and you are the root, the source, the foundation of consciousness. The world is but a succession of experiences and you are what makes them conscious, and yet remain beyond all experience. It is like the heat, the flame and the burning wood. The heat maintains the flame, the flame consumes the wood. Without heat there would be neither flame nor fuel. Similarly, without awareness there would be no consciousness, nor life, which transforms matter into a vehicle of consciousness.

The confusion is apparent and purely verbal. What is, is. It is neither subjective nor objective. Matter and mind are not separate, they are aspects of one energy. Look at the mind as a function of matter and you have science; look at matter as the product of the mind and you have religion.

Neither comes first. for neither appears alone. Matter is the shape, mind is the name. Together they make the world. Pervading and transcending is Reality, pure being -- awareness -- bliss, your very essence.
It is a matter of daily experience that on waking up the world suddenly appears. Where does it come from?
Before waking up I was unconscious.
Before anything can come into being there must be somebody to whom it comes. All appearance and disappearance presupposes a change against some changeless background.
In what sense? Having forgotten, or not having experienced? Don’t you experience even when unconscious? Can you exist without knowing?
A lapse in memory: is it a proof of non-existence? And can you validly talk about your own non-existence as an actual experience?
Did you not wake up on being called? And on waking up, was it not the sense ‘I am’ that came first?
On waking up the experience runs: ‘I am -- the body -- in the world.’ It may appear to arise in succession but in fact it is all simultaneous, a single idea of having a body in a world.
Can there be the sense of ‘I am’ without being somebody or other?
What benefit is there in knowing that I am not the body?
Then what am I?
Even to say that you are not the body is not quite true. In a way you are all the bodies, hearts and minds and much more.
Go deep into the sense of ‘I am’ and you will find.
The sense of being, of 'I am' is the first to emerge. Ask yourself whence it comes, or just watch it quietly.
When the mind stays in the 'I am' without moving, you enter a state which cannot be verbalised but can be experienced.
It is enough to know what you are not. You need not know what you are.
All you can say is: ‘I am not this, I am not that’. You cannot meaningfully say ‘this is what I am’.
The sense of being an experiencer, the sense of ‘I am’, is it not also an experience?
How do I get at it?
Obviously, every thing experienced is an experience. And in every experience there arises the experiencer of it.
Memory creates the illusion of continuity.
In reality each experience has its own experiencer and the sense of identity is due to the common factor at the root of all experiencer–experience relations.
You need not get at it, for you are it. It will get at you, if you give it a chance.
Let go your attachment to the unreal and the real will swiftly and smoothly step into its own.
Still, you are different. Your mind seems to be always quiet and happy. And miracles happen round you.
What do you see?
I know nothing about miracles… As to my mind, there is no such thing. There is consciousness in which everything happens.
You give no attention to your self. Bring your self into focus, become aware of your own existence.
See how you function, watch the motives and the results of your actions. Study the prison you have built around yourself by inadvertence.
By knowing what you are not, you come to know your self.
What has gone wrong is the ‘inner body’, call it mind, consciousness, antahkarana, whatever the name.
It is restless, greedy of the pleasant and afraid of the unpleasant.
What do you consider to be wrong with your mind?

Between the banks of pain and pleasure the river of life flows. It is only when the mind refuses to flow with life… that it becomes a problem. Desire not, fear not, observe the actual, as and when it happens, for you are not what happens, you are to whom it happens. Ultimately even the observer you are not. You are the ultimate potentiality of which the all-embracing consciousness is the manifestation
Even when a man is killed?
The calamity is of the killer.
Still, it seems there are two worlds, mine and yours.
Mine is real, yours is of the mind.
You give no attention to your self. Your mind is all with things, people and ideas, never with your self.
See how you function, watch the motives and the results of your actions.
Study the prison you have built around yourself by inadvertence.
You give no attention to your self. Your mind is all with things, people and ideas, never with your self.
See how you function, watch the motives and the results of your actions.
Study the prison you have built around yourself by inadvertence.
From the relative point of view, everything must have a cause.
Of what use is all this?
Let come what comes and let go what goes — why catch hold of things and enquire about their causes?
If I create the world, why have I made it bad?
What determines the difference?
That's what you say! Did God come and tell you that the world is His creation and concern and not yours?
You know. Everybody knows.
It cannot be so bad! I exist in your world as you exist in mine.
Everyone lives in his own world. Not all the worlds are equally good or bad.
The mind that projects the world, colours it its own way. When you meet a man, he is a stranger.
Consider. The world in which you live, who else knows about it?
Did anybody come from outside of your world to tell you? Myself and everybody else appear and disappear in your world. We are all at your mercy.
You have no evidence of my world. You are completely wrapped up in the world of your own making.
So all my questions, my search and study are of no use?
How am I to get a true answer?
These are but the stirrings of a man who is tired of sleeping. They are not the causes of awakening, but its early signs. But, you must not ask idle questions, to which you already know the answers.
By asking a true question -- non-verbally, but by daring to live according to your lights. A man willing to die for truth will get it.
You always tell us to rely on the inner Guru. Then why do you sit here and allow us to worship your form?
Yet when I come here and sit near you, I feel quiet and full. Away from you I lose it.
So the Guru does nothing for the disciple?
How do I know that inner presence is not just my imagination?
If you only worship this form, you are wasting your time. If this form reminds you of your own true nature, then it has done its work, and you can forget it.

Here you forget your usual stories about yourself, so peace appears. Away from here you remember them again and call it 'losing peace'. The peace is not mine; it is what remains when you stop disturbing yourself.
The Guru is a function: to reveal your own Guru. When you see that the same presence shines in you, this old man in front of you is no longer needed.
Imagination comes and goes and needs effort to be maintained. This presence is there before imagination and after it, quietly knowing. Trust what does not need to be produced.
Sometimes everything feels meaningless. Even spiritual talk becomes just more words. Is there any point to all this?
So my boredom is useful?
But when I do that, it feels flat and dull.
Will this 'I am' ever become blissful like the scriptures promise?
Good. When your toys bore you, you begin to look at the child. When all meanings feel empty, you are close to what does not need meaning.
If you use it. Instead of running to new entertainments, stay with the naked sense 'I am' that remains when everything else is tasteless. That is the doorway.
It feels dull because you are comparing it with the excitement of becoming. Drop the comparison. The 'dullness' is only the mind complaining that it has nothing to play with.
It does not become anything. When you stop demanding experiences from it, its quiet joy becomes obvious. You do not find it by decoration, but by subtraction.

You were telling us that there are many self-styled Gurus, but a real Guru is very rare. There are many jnani who imagine themselves realised, but all they have is book knowledge and a high opinion of themselves. Sometimes they impress, even fascinate, attract disciples and make them waste their time in useless practices. After some years, when the disciple takes stock of himself, he finds no change. When he complains to his teacher, he gets the usual rebuke that he did not try hard enough. The blame is on the lack of faith and love in the heart of the disciple, while in reality the blame is on the Guru, who had no business in accepting disciples and raising their hopes. How to protect oneself from such Gurus?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Why be so concerned with others? Whoever may be the Guru, if he is pure of heart and acts in good faith, he will do his disciples no harm. If there is no progress, the fault lies with the disciples, their laziness and lack of self-control. On the other hand, if the disciple is earnest and applies himself intelligently and with zest to his sadhana, he is bound to meet a more qualified teacher, who will take him further. Your question flows from three false assumptions: that one needs concern oneself with others; that one can evaluate another and that the progress of the disciple is the task and responsibility of his Guru. In reality, the Guru's role is only to instruct and encourage; the disciple is totally responsible for himself.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: We are told that total surrender to the Guru is enough, that the Guru will do the rest.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Of course, when there is total surrender, complete relinquishment of all concern with one's past, presents and future, with one's physical and spiritual security and standing, a new life dawns, full of love and beauty; then the Guru is not important, for the disciple has broken the shell of self-defence. Complete self-surrender by itself is liberation.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: When both the disciple and his teacher are inadequate, what will happen?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: In the long run all will be well. After all, the real Self of both is not affected by the comedy they play for a time. They will sober up and ripen and shift to a higher level of relationship.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Or, they may separate.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Yes, they may separate. After all, no relationship is forever. Duality is a temporary state.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Is it by accident that I met you and by another accident shall we separate never to meet again? Or is my meeting you a part of some cosmic pattern, a fragment in the great drama of our lives?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: The real is meaningful and the meaningful relates to reality. If our relationship is meaningful to you and me, it cannot be accidental. The future affects the present as much, as the past.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: How can I make out who is a real saint and who is not?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: You cannot, unless you have a clear insight into the heart of man. Appearances are deceptive. To see clearly, your mind must be pure and unattached. Unless you know yourself well, how can you know another? And when you know yourself -- you are the other. Leave others alone for some time and examine yourself. There are so many things you do not know about yourself -- what are you, who are you, how did you come to be born, what are you doing now and why, where are you going, what is the meaning and purpose of your life, your death, your future? Have you a past, have you a future? How did you come to live in turmoil and sorrow, while your entire being strives for happiness and peace? These are weighty matters and have to be attended to first. You have no need, nor time for finding who is a jnani and who is not?
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: This infinite and eternal self of mine, how am I to know it?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: The self you want to know, is it some second self? Are you made of several selves? Surely, there is only one self and you are that self. The self you are is the only self there is. Remove and abandon your wrong ideas about yourself and there it is, in all its glory. It is only your mind that prevents self-knowledge.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: How am I to be rid of the mind? And is life without mind at all possible on the human level?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: There is no such thing as mind. There are ideas and some of them are wrong. Abandon the wrong ideas, for they are false and obstruct your vision of yourself.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Which ideas are wrong and which are true?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Assertions are usually wrong and denials -- right.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: One cannot live by denying everything!
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Only by denying can one live. Assertion is bondage. To question and deny is necessary. It is the essence of revolt and without revolt there can be no freedom. There is no second, or higher self to search for. You are the highest self, only give up the false ideas you have about your self. Both faith and reason tell you that you are neither the body, nor its desires and fears, nor are you the mind with its fanciful ideas, nor the role society compels you to play, the person you are supposed to be. Give up the false and the true will come into its own. You say you want to know your self. You are your self -- you cannot be anything but what you are. Is knowing separate from being? Whatever you can know with your mind is of the mind, not you; about yourself you can only say: 'I am, I am aware, I like It'.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: I find being alive a painful state.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: You cannot be alive for you are life itself. It is the person you imagine yourself to be that suffers, not you. Dissolve it in awareness. It is merely a bundle of memories and habits. From the awareness of the unreal to the awareness of your real nature there is a chasm which you will easily cross, once you have mastered the art of pure awareness.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: All I know is that I do not know myself.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: How do you know, that you do not know your self? Your direct insight tells you that yourself you know first, for nothing exists to you without your being there to experience its existence. You imagine you do not know your self, because you cannot describe your self. You can always say: 'I know that I am' and you will refuse as untrue the statement: 'I am not'. But whatever can be described cannot be your self, and what you are cannot be described. You can only know your self by being yourself without any attempt at self-definition and self-description. Once you have understood that you are nothing perceivable or conceivable, that whatever appears in the field of consciousness cannot be your self, you will apply yourself to the eradication of all self-identification, as the only way that can take you to a deeper realisation of your self. You literally progress by rejection -- a veritable rocket. To know that you are neither in the body nor in the mind, though aware of both, is already self-knowledge.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: If I am neither the body nor mind, how am I aware of them? How can I perceive something quite foreign to myself?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: 'Nothing is me,' is the first step. 'Everything is me' is the next. Both hang on the idea: 'there is a world'. When this too is given up, you remain what you are -- the non-dual Self. You are it here and now, but your vision is obstructed by your false ideas about your self.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: What is the cause of desire and fear?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Obviously, the memory of past pains and pleasures. There is no great mystery about it. Conflict arises only when desire and fear refer to the same object.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: How to put an end to memory?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: It is neither necessary, nor possible. realise that all happens in consciousness and you are the root, the source, the foundation of consciousness. The world is but a succession of experiences and you are what makes them conscious, and yet remain beyond all experience. It is like the heat, the flame and the burning wood. The heat maintains the flame, the flame consumes the wood. Without heat there would be neither flame nor fuel. Similarly, without awareness there would be no consciousness, nor life, which transforms matter into a vehicle of consciousness.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: You maintain that without me there would be no world, and that the world and my knowledge of the world are identical. Science has come to a quite different conclusion: the world exists as something concrete and continuous, while I am a by-product of biological evolution of the nervous system, which is primarily not so much a seat of consciousness, as a mechanism of survival as individual and species. Yours is altogether a subjective view, while science tries to describe everything in objective terms. Is this contradiction inevitable?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: The confusion is apparent and purely verbal. What is, is. It is neither subjective nor objective. Matter and mind are not separate, they are aspects of one energy. Look at the mind as a function of matter and you have science; look at matter as the product of the mind and you have religion.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: But what is true? What comes first, mind or matter?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Neither comes first. for neither appears alone. Matter is the shape, mind is the name. Together they make the world. Pervading and transcending is Reality, pure being -- awareness -- bliss, your very essence.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: What does it mean, nothing is? Do you turn blank, or go to sleep? Or do you dissolve the world and keep us all in abeyance, until we are brought back to life at the next flicker of your thought?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Oh, no, it is not that bad. The world of mind and matter, of names and shapes, continues, but it does not matter to me at all. It is like having a shadow. It is there -- following me wherever I go, but not hindering me in any way. It remains a world of experiences, but not of names and forms related to me by desires and fears. The experiences are qualityless, pure experiences, if I may say so. I call them experiences for the lack of a better word. They are like the waves on the surface of the ocean, the ever-present, but not affecting its peaceful power.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: You mean to say an experience can be nameless, formless, undefined?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: In the beginning all experience is such. It is only desire and fear, born of memory, that give it name and form and separate it from other experiences. It is not a conscious experience, for it is not in opposition to other experiences, yet it is an experience all the same.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: If it is not conscious, why talk about it?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Most of your experiences are unconscious. The conscious ones are very few. You are unaware of the fact because to you only the conscious ones count. Become aware of the unconscious .
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Can one be aware of the unconscious? How is it done?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Desire and fear are the obscuring and distorting factors. When mind is free of them the unconscious becomes accessible.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Does it mean that the unconscious becomes conscious?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: It is rather the other way round. The conscious becomes one with the unconscious. The distinction ceases, whichever way you look at it.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: I am puzzled. How can one be aware and yet unconscious?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Awareness is not limited to consciousness. It is of all that is. Consciousness is of duality. There is no duality in awareness. It is one single block of pure cognition. In the same way one can talk of the pure being and pure creation -- nameless, formless, silent and yet absolutely real, powerful, effective. Their being indescribable does not affect them in the least. While they are unconscious, they are essential. The conscious cannot change fundamentally, it can only modify. Any thing, to change, must pass through death, through obscuration and dissolution. Gold jewellery must be melted down before it is cast into another shape. What refuses to die cannot be reborn.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Master Gotama, does the Tathāgata exist after death?
turns.speaker: Vacchagotta

turns.text: Vaccha, that does not apply.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then, Master Gotama, does the Tathāgata not exist after death?
turns.speaker: Vacchagotta

turns.text: Vaccha, that does not apply.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then is it that the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death?
turns.speaker: Vacchagotta

turns.text: Vaccha, that does not apply.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: But Master Gotama, when a fire goes out, is it correct to say that the fire has gone east, west, north, or south?
turns.speaker: Vacchagotta

turns.text: Vaccha, the question does not apply. The fire depended on fuel. When that fuel is used up, it is said to be 'out' through lack of fuel.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then how should I understand the disappearance of the fire, Master Gotama?
turns.speaker: Vacchagotta

turns.text: In the same way, Vaccha, all terms for the Tathāgata after death do not apply. Freed from reckoning by form, feeling, perception, fabrications, or consciousness, he is deep, immeasurable, unfathomable — like the ocean.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then, Master Gotama, is there a self?
turns.speaker: Vacchagotta

turns.text: Vaccha, if I were to say 'there is a self,' you would be aligned with the eternalists.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then, Master Gotama, is there no self?
turns.speaker: Vacchagotta

turns.text: If I were to say 'there is no self,' you would fall into confusion: 'Formerly I had a self; now I have no self at all.'
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Vaccha, this question is not answered because you are not yet ready for the grasping to be stilled.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then why, Master Gotama, do you not declare these things plainly?
turns.speaker: Vacchagotta

turns.text: Vaccha, if I were to answer in your terms, it would not lead to dispassion, to peace, to cessation, to direct knowledge, to awakening.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: So Master Gotama leaves me uncertain and without ground.
turns.speaker: Vacchagotta

turns.text: Vaccha, it is precisely your ground that must be seen as groundless.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then I will consider this further, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Vacchagotta

turns.text: I will question the ascetic Gotama. If he answers me well, so much the better. If he does not, I will shake him, agitate him, pull him about, as a strong man might shake a feeble goat!
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: But what is your doctrine, Aggivessana? What is it that you hold?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Form, Master Gotama, is the self. Feeling is the self. Perception is the self. Fabrications are the self. Consciousness is the self.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: Do you say, Aggivessana, that all five aggregates are the self?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Exactly so, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: Aggivessana, is form permanent or impermanent?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Impermanent, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: Is what is impermanent easeful or stressful?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Stressful, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: Is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, stressful, subject to change, as ‘This is mine; this is my self; this is what I am’?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: No indeed, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: Aggivessana, did you not say that form is the self?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: I did, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: But now, Aggivessana, you admit it is impermanent, stressful, subject to change, and cannot rightly be regarded as self. How can both of your claims stand?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: And at that moment, Saccaka, the debater, broke into a sweat, as if water were streaming from his body.
turns.speaker: Narrator

turns.text: Aggivessana, your doctrine is being pressed. Take care.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Master Gotama, let us set aside form. Let us discuss feeling...
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: Aggivessana, we will not move on until we settle what has already been said.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: But Master Gotama, I wish to proceed.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: Aggivessana, when you made your claim, you stood upon it. Now that it falters, you try to flee. But the matter must be resolved here.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then proceed, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: Aggivessana, is feeling permanent or impermanent?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Impermanent, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: Is perception permanent or impermanent?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Impermanent, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: And fabrications, consciousness — are they permanent or impermanent?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Impermanent, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: Then, Aggivessana, is it fitting to regard any of these as ‘This is mine; this is my self; this is what I am’?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: No indeed, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Saccaka

turns.text: Form is not-self. For if form were self, it would not lead to affliction, and one could say: 'Let my form be thus.' But you cannot.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Feeling is not-self. If feeling were self, it would not oppress, and one could command it. But it does not obey.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Perception is not-self. If it were self, it would not shift and change against your will.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Fabrications are not-self. They arise and pass without regard for your wishes.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Consciousness is not-self. If it were self, it would not alter. But it flickers and fades.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Seeing this with wisdom, the instructed disciple becomes disenchanted. Disenchantment leads to fading. Fading leads to release.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Monks, the eye is burning. Forms are burning. Eye-consciousness is burning. Eye-contact is burning.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Burning with what? Burning with the fire of greed, the fire of hatred, the fire of delusion.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: The ear is burning. Sounds are burning. The nose is burning. Smells are burning. The mind is burning. Thoughts are burning.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Seeing this, the instructed disciple becomes disenchanted with the sense fields. Through disenchantment comes fading. Through fading comes release.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: While this discourse was being spoken, the hearts of a thousand monks were liberated.
turns.speaker: NARRATION

turns.text: Lady, what is feeling?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: There are three feelings, friend Visakha: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: But Lady, what is the cause and condition for feeling?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: Contact, friend Visakha, is the cause and condition for feeling.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: But Lady, what is the cause and condition for contact?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: Name-and-form is the condition for contact.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: Lady, what is the cause and condition for craving?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: Feeling, friend Visakha, is the cause and condition for craving.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: And what is the cause and condition for feeling?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: Contact is the condition for feeling.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: And for contact?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: Name-and-form is the condition for contact.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: Lady, what is the cessation of craving?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: The ending of craving, the abandonment of craving, the relinquishing of craving—this, friend Visakha, is the cessation of craving.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: And what is the path leading to the cessation of craving?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: The Noble Eightfold Path leads to the cessation of craving.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: And what is the Noble Eightfold Path?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: Lady, what is the self? And what is not-self?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: Form, friend Visakha, is not self. Feeling is not self. Perception is not self. Fabrications are not self. Consciousness is not self.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: Lady, why are these not self?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: Because, friend Visakha, they are impermanent, changing, subject to decay.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: Is there, then, any self?
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: Visakha, that is a matter for the Tathāgata.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: But tell me now, friend Visakha—what is feeling?
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: Lady, feeling is pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: And what is the cause of feeling?
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: Contact is the cause of feeling.
turns.speaker: Visakha

turns.text: Good, Visakha. You have understood well.
turns.speaker: Dhammadinna

turns.text: There are thoughts of sensuality, ill will, and cruelty. And there are thoughts of renunciation, goodwill, and harmlessness.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: When I directed my mind to thoughts of sensuality, I understood: 'This thought leads to my own harm, to the harm of others, and to the harm of both.'
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Knowing this, such a thought is to be abandoned.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: When I directed my mind to thoughts of renunciation, I understood: 'This leads to my welfare, the welfare of others, and the welfare of both.'
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Knowing this, such a thought is to be cultivated.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Thus I sorted thoughts into two classes: those to be abandoned and those to be developed.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: He systematically divided and trained his mind in this way.
turns.speaker: NARRATION

turns.text: When unskillful thoughts arise, one should replace them with a skillful counterpart.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: If that does not calm the mind, one should attend to the danger in the unskillful thought.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: If that does not calm it, one should ignore and forget the thought.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: If that does not calm it, one should relax the formation of the thought itself.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: If that does not calm it, one should crush the mind with the mind, restraining it.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: A mind so trained becomes steady and settled.
turns.speaker: NARRATION

turns.text: Rahula, any action you wish to do with body, speech, or mind should be examined again and again, just as one looks into a mirror.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: If, on reflection, you know: 'This action would lead to harm for myself or others,' then such an action should not be done.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: But if, upon reflection, you know: 'This action would lead to no harm,' then it is fitting to do it.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: And having done an action, you should reflect: 'Did this action lead to harm?'
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: If it did, confess it, reveal it, make amends, and train yourself not to repeat it.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: If it did not lead to harm, you may rest easy, and continue training in wholesome qualities.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Yes, sir.
turns.speaker: RAHULA

turns.text: Kesi, you are a trainer of horses. How do you train them?
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Lord, I train them first with gentleness. If that fails, with firmness. If that fails, with both. And if a horse cannot be tamed by any method, I end its life.
turns.speaker: KESI

turns.text: So too, Kesi, I train by gentleness, by firmness, and by a blend of both.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: But if a person cannot be tamed by any method, I do not end their life. I simply do not instruct them further.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: It is better to let such a person go than to waste training on one who refuses to learn.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: It is wonderful, lord, how you train people without causing harm.
turns.speaker: KESI

turns.text: Master Gotama, this is my view: ‘I take no view. Nothing is acceptable to me.’
turns.speaker: Dighanakha

turns.text: Aggivessana, do you hold that view as true?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Yes, Master Gotama, this is truly my view.
turns.speaker: Dighanakha

turns.text: But if you take that as true, then at least this one view is acceptable to you.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Master Gotama, it seems this view does not stand as I thought.
turns.speaker: Dighanakha

turns.text: When one says ‘Nothing is acceptable to me,’ that itself is something accepted.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: And Dighanakha’s view was thereby shaken.
turns.speaker: Narrator

turns.text: Aggivessana, there are three kinds of views: ‘Everything is pleasing to me,’ ‘Nothing is pleasing to me,’ and ‘Some things are pleasing to me and some are not.’
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Master Gotama, how does this apply to one who claims that nothing is acceptable?
turns.speaker: Dighanakha

turns.text: One who says that nothing is acceptable is bound by that view, and thus is not free from clinging.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: So even rejecting all things creates a bond?
turns.speaker: Dighanakha

turns.text: Indeed. To grasp the idea ‘nothing is acceptable’ is itself a form of clinging.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Aggivessana, when you experience a pleasant feeling, is it permanent or impermanent?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Impermanent, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Dighanakha

turns.text: And unpleasant feelings—permanent or impermanent?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Impermanent, Master Gotama.
turns.speaker: Dighanakha

turns.text: Neutral feelings—permanent or impermanent?
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Impermanent as well.
turns.speaker: Dighanakha

turns.text: Aggivessana, when one sees the arising of feeling, its passing away, and its change while it persists—then one is not bound by feeling.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Master Gotama, how should one attend to such seeing?
turns.speaker: Dighanakha

turns.text: Attend simply as ‘feeling arises, feeling remains, feeling passes away.’ When one sees this, there is no ‘I’ in feeling.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: So one stands apart from it?
turns.speaker: Dighanakha

turns.text: Just so. One stands as the watcher, not the owned.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: And as the Blessed One spoke this teaching, Dighanakha’s mind was liberated from the fetter of views.
turns.speaker: Narrator

turns.text: Master Gotama, marvelous indeed are these teachings.
turns.speaker: Dighanakha

turns.text: When views are abandoned, Aggivessana, one knows directly what arises and ceases.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Venerable sir, what is right view?
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: Kaccana, by and large, this world is supported by a duality: by existence and by non-existence.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: How does this duality bind the world?
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: One who sees the arising of the world as it really is does not hold the view of non-existence. One who sees the cessation of the world as it really is does not hold the view of existence.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then right view avoids both?
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: Indeed. Right view is free from these two extremes.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Kaccana, this world is mostly bound by clinging, taking hold of something or other.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: What is the view that abandons clinging?
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: When one sees dependent origination as it is—‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises’—one does not cling to any view of existence or non-existence.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: So right view is seeing conditions?
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: Just so. Seeing conditional arising and conditional cessation.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: This seems a middle way beyond views.
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: It is the middle by which the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Venerable sir, how does one see rightly?
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: By seeing that all is merely arising and ceasing.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: And seeing this, what does one abandon?
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: One abandons the thought ‘I am’ in regard to these processes.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: So the sense of self depends on misunderstanding the process?
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: Just so. Where there is arising and ceasing, no self is found.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Venerable sir, should one say ‘there is a self’?
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: Kaccana, saying ‘there is a self’ is one extreme.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then should one say ‘there is no self’?
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: Saying ‘there is no self’ is the other extreme.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Then how should the matter be seen?
turns.speaker: Kaccanagotta

turns.text: With right wisdom seeing only arising and ceasing.
turns.speaker: The Buddha

turns.text: Lord, different teachers come to Kesaputta. Each declares his own doctrine true and condemns the others. We are confused and in doubt.
turns.speaker: KALAMAS

turns.text: It is fitting that you are in doubt, Kalamas. Doubt has arisen about matters that are doubtful.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Do not go by reports, traditions, or legends. Do not go by the authority of texts.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Do not go by reasoning, by logic, by inference, or by acceptance of a view.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: When you yourselves know: 'These qualities are unwholesome; these qualities are blameworthy; these qualities lead to harm,' then you should abandon them.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: And when you yourselves know: 'These qualities are wholesome; these qualities are blameless; these qualities lead to welfare,' then you should practice them.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Yes, lord. This is clear.
turns.speaker: KALAMAS

turns.text: The Kalamas were uplifted by this teaching.
turns.speaker: NARRATION

turns.text: Socrates, before I even met you I used to hear that you are always in a state of perplexity and that you bring others to the same state, and now I think you are bewitching and beguiling me, simply putting me under a spell, so that I am quite perplexed.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: Indeed, if a joke is in order, you seem, in appearance and in every other way, to be like the broad torpedo fish, for it too makes anyone who comes close and touches it feel numb, and you now seem to have had that kind of effect on me, for both my mind and my tongue are numb, and I have no answer to give you.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: Yet I have made many speeches about virtue before large audiences on a thousand occasions, very good speeches as I thought, but now I cannot even say what it is.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: You are a rascal, Meno, and you nearly deceived me.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Why so particularly, Socrates?
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: Because I know why you likened me to the torpedo fish.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: If I do numb you, it is because I myself am numb, and I cause others to be so; for I do not know what virtue is either.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: I am even more at a loss than you are, and so I share with you only my own perplexity.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: And how will you look for something, Socrates, when you do not know at all what it is?
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: How will you aim to search for something you do not know? If you find it, how will you know that this is what you did not know?
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: You understand what an eristic argument you are bringing up—that a man cannot search either for what he knows or for what he does not know.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: For he cannot search for what he knows—since he knows it—and he cannot search for what he does not know—since he does not know what to look for.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: As it is, we must not believe that this argument is sound.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: I have heard wise men and women speak of divine matters—they include priests and priestesses.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: They say that the soul of man is immortal, and that when one dies, it departs and is born again, and nothing is ever destroyed.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Thus, because the soul has been born many times and has seen all things, there is nothing it has not learned; it is no wonder that it can recollect what it once knew.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Therefore one ought to be courageous and try to discover what one does not presently know, or recollect it.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Can you teach me that this is so, Socrates?
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: I can, if you are willing to follow me closely.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Call one of your attendants, whichever you like, so that I may show you by example.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Certainly.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: Pay close attention, and watch whether he learns or recollects.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Can you tell me, Socrates, can virtue be taught? Or is it not teachable but the result of practice, or is it neither of these, but men possess it by nature or in some other way?
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: Before now, Meno, Thessalians had a high high reputation among the Greeks ... If I do not know what something is, how could I know what qualities it possesses?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Do you really not know what virtue is? Are we to report this to the folk back home about you?
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: Not only that, my friend, but also that, as I believe, I have never yet met anyone else who did know.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: It is not hard to tell you, Socrates. First, if you want the virtue of a man ... and very many others.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: I seem to be in great luck, Meno; while I am looking for one virtue, I have found you to have a whole swarm of them.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: If I were asking you what is the nature of bees ... Tell me, what would you answer?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: I would say that they do not differ from one another in being bees.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: The same is true of virtues. They all share one form. That is what we must seek.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: I am asking whether you think it is only in the case of virtue that there is one for man, another for woman ... does it have the same form everywhere?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: The health of a man seems to me the same as that of a woman.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: And so with size and strength? If a woman is strong ... strength is the same?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: I do not think so.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: So all human beings are good in the same way. They acquire the same qualities.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: What else but to be able to rule over people, if you are seeking one description to fit them all.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: But is this true of children and slaves as well? Should they rule too?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: And should we not add: rule justly and not unjustly?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Certainly—for justice is virtue.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: Is it virtue, Meno, or a virtue? As roundness is a shape, but not shape itself?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Suppose someone asked you: What is shape? And you replied: roundness. Would he not ask: is roundness a shape, or a shape among many?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: I would say it is a shape among many.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: Then you would be asked: what is that in which all shapes share? Speak in terms known to your questioner, not in clever disputations.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: I think I understand what you mean.
turns.speaker: MENO

turns.text: Shape is the boundary of a solid. That is a definition in common terms.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Tell me, boy, do you know that a square figure is like this?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Yes.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: And that a square has all these four equal sides?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Yes.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: And has it not also equal lines drawn across it through the middle?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Yes.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: Now if this side is two feet, and this other side is also two, how many feet will the whole be?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Four.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: And if one wished to make another square double its size, how long would each of its sides be?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Plainly, Socrates, twice the length.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: You say that a square double in area must have sides twice as long?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Yes.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: Let us see. If the side becomes twice as long, it will be four feet, will it not?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Yes.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: Then the area will be sixteen feet, will it not? For four times four is sixteen.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: It seems so.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: But you were saying that double the area would be eight?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Yes.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: So it is not by doubling the side that one gets a double area.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: That is true.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: Now tell me: if the double area is not produced by doubling the side, what length should the side be?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: I do not know.
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: You see, Meno, he is now in the state of not knowing.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: And yet, formerly he thought he knew and answered confidently.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Now he is perplexed and numbed like he was before, yet he is better off about the matter he did not know.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Observe then whether the side of the double square might not be this diagonal.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: What is a diagonal?
turns.speaker: SLAVE

turns.text: It is the line drawn from one corner to the opposite corner of the square.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Yes, I know that.
turns.speaker: SLAVE
