You cannot eliminate it. It is just the same as trying to cut your head off. But you
can make it less insistent, less permanent... If, at a certain moment, you feel the
danger of a manifestation of false personality and you find a way to stop it, this is what
you have to begin with. The question of elimination does not enter at all... You must have control.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Could one stop having impressions if one wanted to?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
No, certainly not. You cannot stop impressions altogether, but... you can
keep off undesirable impressions and attract to yourself another kind of impressions... For instance, people stand in the street looking at a street accident, and then talk about
it until the next accident. These people collect wrong impressions.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
You have to think not so much about choosing the right
impressions as about isolating yourself from wrong impressions. Only by doing this
will you have a certain control. If you try to choose right impressions, you will only
deceive yourself. So, although you cannot bring desirable impressions to yourself, you
can... learn to control them by isolating yourself from
certain kinds of wrong impressions.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: Do you think there is anything in telepathy?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
For men 1, 2 and 3 it does not exist at all;
it is imagination. But men of a much
higher development control forces which can produce so-called telepathy... But ordinary mind and ordinary
emotions cannot do it.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
I wonder by what process Jesus was able to expel devils and whether anything in
the system could be used for similar purpose? Has it anything to do with higher
centres?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Jesus probably dealt with big devils. We have to begin with small devils—a kind of
vivisection—until we are able to deal with big devils.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: I do not understand about the speed of emotions. How can it be measured?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
By realizing how many different feelings can pass in you during one thought or
during one swing of the pendulum.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
By speed of emotions do you mean the time between the cause and effect of an
emotion?
turns.speaker: Questioner
Teacher

turns.text: The rate varies according to the degree of consciousness?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Your observation will vary... But, as I said, the emotional centre in us does not work with its
proper speed, because mostly only the moving parts of it work;
and when a centre
works with the moving part its speed is much slower, whereas when it works with the
intellectual part it is much quicker.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: I find that I work for immediate results. Is it a wrong aim?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
There is no question of right and wrong: there is only the question of knowing your
aim. Aim must always be in the present and refer to the future.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: How can one see how to make big efforts?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
By making small efforts. You
cannot begin with big efforts. You must begin with small efforts, like, for instance,
trying to remember yourself, or trying to stop thoughts three times a day. It is quite a
small effort, but if you do it regularly, the need or the possibility of a big effort may
come.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text:
When I first came to lectures, I had a very large aim, but now it has got much
smaller.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text:
Yes, aims shrink very much when you begin to work. They start enormous—like
balloons—and then they become quite small, so that you can put them in your pocket.
turns.speaker: Teacher

turns.text: If the substance of the auspicious things was not produced in dependence on anything, there would be no religious practice. There would be neither right nor wrong nor worldly conventions.
turns.speaker: Realist

turns.text: They would be permanent and substantial; because they are permanent they are acausal. [cite_start]While there is no cause there is no arising, remaining, and decay. [cite: 2552, 2563]
turns.speaker: Nagarjuna

turns.text: In this context, the non-existence of religious practice would follow exactly. And there is a contradiction with your own position. Why? [cite_start]Because the Blessed One said that all compounded things are impermanent. [cite: 2557-2558]
turns.speaker: Nagarjuna

turns.text: And if there was no substance, there would also not even be the name "insubstantiality of things," for there is no name without a referent.
turns.speaker: Realist

turns.text: The name "non-existent"—what is this, something existent or again something non-existent? [cite_start]For if it is existent or if it is nonexistent, either way your position is deficient. [cite: 2572-2573]
turns.speaker: Nagarjuna

turns.text: If in this context the name "non-existent" is the name of an existent, to that extent the thesis is abandoned. [cite_start]Moreover, if the name "non-existent" is the name of a non-existent—there is no name of something which does not exist. [cite: 2575-2577]
turns.speaker: Nagarjuna

turns.text: If that statement [of yours] exists substantially, your earlier thesis is refuted. There is an inequality to be explained, and the specific reason for this should be given.
turns.speaker: Realist

turns.text: Moreover, you could think that there should not be this mistake by arguing, "This statement exists substantially and because it is a substance it is not empty. [cite_start]Therefore it negates the substance of all things." We say in reply: If it is like this, your earlier thesis that all things are empty is refuted. [cite: 19-22]
turns.speaker: Realist

turns.text: This speech does not exist substantially, therefore there is no destruction of my position. [cite_start]There is no inequality, and no particular reason to be mentioned. [cite: 161-162]
turns.speaker: Nagarjuna

turns.text: As far as my speech is empty and all the other things are also empty, there is no inequality. If we say "this speech is not empty, yet all the other things are empty," there would be an inequality. [cite_start]But it is not like this. [cite: 165-167]
turns.speaker: Nagarjuna

turns.text: To the extent to which the negation "there is no pot in the house" is precisely a negation of an existent, your negation is a negation of an existing substance.
turns.speaker: Realist

turns.text: Thus the statement "there is no pot in the house" brings about the negation of an existent, not of a non-existent pot. [cite_start]Just in this way, the statement "there is no substance of things" achieves the negation of an existent substance. [cite: 95-98]
turns.speaker: Realist

turns.text: If negation is of an existent thing, is it not that emptiness is established? Because you negate the insubstantiality of things.
turns.speaker: Nagarjuna

turns.text: If negation is of an existent thing and not of a non-existent one, and if you negate the insubstantiality of all things, is it not that the insubstantiality of all things is established? [cite_start]Your speech, which is a negation, establishes emptiness because it is the negation of the insubstantiality of all things. [cite: 351-353]
turns.speaker: Nagarjuna

turns.text: If, sire, you walk at noon-time on the hot scorching ground, trampling on sharp grit, pebbles and sand, your feet will hurt you, your body will be tired, your mind will be disturbed and you will suffer bodily pain. Now, did you come on foot or in a vehicle?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: I, revered sir, did not come on foot. I came in a chariot.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: If, sire, you came in a chariot, show me the chariot. Is the pole the chariot, sire?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Is the axle the chariot?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Are the wheels the chariot?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Then, sire, are the pole, the axle, the wheels, the body, the flag-staff, the yoke, the reins, the goad all together the chariot?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Well then, sire, is the chariot apart from the pole, the axle, the wheels, the body, the flag-staff, the yoke, the reins and the goad?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, sire.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Sire, though I have been asking you repeatedly, I do not see this chariot. Chariot is only a sound. What then is the chariot you say you came in? You, sire, have spoken a falsehood, an untruth. There is no chariot.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: I am not, revered sir, speaking a lie. It is because of the pole, because of the axle, the wheels, the body, the flag-staff, the yoke, the reins and because of the goad that ‘chariot’ exists as a mere designation.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: It is good, sire, that you understand a chariot. Even so is it for me, sire, because of the hairs of the head … because of the urine, because of material form … because of consciousness, that ‘Nāgasena’ exists as a mere designation. However, in the ultimate sense there is no person as such that is found.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, will you converse with me?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: I will converse if you, sire, will converse in the speech of the learned, but if you converse in the speech of kings I will not converse.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: How, revered Nāgasena, do the learned converse?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: When the learned are conversing, sire, there is a turning over and an unravelling of the subject; then there is a refutation and an acknowledgement of a mistake; distinctions and contradistinctions are drawn; yet, thereby, they are not angered. It is thus, sire, that the learned converse.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: And how, revered sir, do kings converse?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: When kings are conversing, sire, they approve of some matter and order punishment for anyone who disagrees with that matter, saying: ‘Inflict a punishment on him.’ It is thus, sire, that kings converse.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: I, revered sir, will converse in the speech of the learned, not in the speech of kings. Let the revered one converse unreservedly as he converses with a monk or a novice or a lay follower or with a monastery attendant. Let the revered one converse thus, let him not be afraid.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, is he who uprises the same or is he another?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Neither the same nor another. What do you think about this, sire? Now that you are grown up are you the same as you were when you were a boy, young, tender, lying on your back?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir. That boy, young, tender, lying on his back was one thing. I, who am now full-grown, am another.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: That being so, sire, you can have no mother, nor can you have a father, nor can you have a teacher... It is one ‘I’ that was the boy, young, tender, lying on his back and it is the same ‘I’ that am now full-grown, and all these are held together as a unity in dependence on this body itself.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Make a simile.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: It is as if, sire, some person might light a lamp. Would it burn all night long?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Yes, revered sir, it might burn all night long.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Is the flame of the first watch of the night the same as the flame of the middle watch?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Is the flame of the middle watch the same as the flame of the third watch?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Is it then, sire, that the lamp in the first watch was one thing, the lamp in the middle watch another, and the lamp in the third watch still another?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir, it was burning all through the night in dependence on itself.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Even so, sire, a continuity of phenomena is linked together. It uprises as one and ceases as another, linked together as though there were no before and no after. Hence it is neither the same nor another, but the subsequent consciousness is reckoned (together with) the preceding consciousness.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, who takes rebirth?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Mind-and-matter, sire, takes rebirth.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: What, is it this same mind-and-matter itself that takes rebirth?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: This same mind-and-matter does not itself take rebirth, sire; but, sire, by means of this mind-and-matter one does a good or bad deed and, because of this deed, another mind-and-matter takes rebirth.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: If, revered sir, this mind-and-matter itself does not take rebirth would one not be freed from evil deeds?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: If, sire, it did not take rebirth one would be freed from evil deeds. But because, sire, it takes rebirth one is not freed from evil deeds. ... Suppose, sire, some man were to steal another man’s mangoes and the owner of the mangoes were to seize him and bring him before the king... and he were to say, ‘Your majesty, I did not steal his mangoes; the mangoes he planted were different from these that I stole; I do not deserve punishment.’ Would he, sire, not deserve punishment?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Yes, revered sir, he would deserve punishment.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: For what reason?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Whatever he may say, the mangoes he stole resulted from the mangoes which, he admits, the other man planted.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Even so, sire, by means of this mind-and-matter one does a good or bad deed and, because of this deed, another mind-and-matter takes rebirth; therefore, one is not freed from evil deeds.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, is there such a thing as an experiencer?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: What does this ‘experiencer’ mean, sire?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: A soul within that sees a visible form with the eye, hears a sound with the ear... Just as we who are sitting here in the palace can look out of any window we want to look out of, even so, revered sir, this soul within can look out of any door it wants to look out of.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: I will talk to you, sire, about the five doors. Listen and attend carefully. If the soul within sees a visible form through the eye just as we who are sitting here in the palace can look out of any window we want to look out of... can it not hear a sound, smell a smell, taste a taste, feel a touch and discriminate mental states through each of the other five doors besides the one you have specified in each case?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Again, sire, we who are sitting here in the palace will see visible forms out there before us more clearly in the great space if these network windows are removed. Thus too, would this soul within see visible forms more clearly when the doors of the eyes are removed? And if the ears were removed, the nose removed, the tongue removed, the body removed, would it hear a sound, smell a smell, taste a taste and feel a touch more clearly on account of the great space?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Because, sire, of the eye and visible form eye-consciousness arises. ... Thus these things are produced from a condition and there is no experiencer found here.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, will you converse with me?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: I will converse if you, sire, will converse in the speech of the learned, but if you converse in the speech of kings I will not converse.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: How, revered Nāgasena, do the learned converse?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: When the learned are conversing, sire, there is a turning over and an unravelling of the subject; then there is a refutation and an acknowledgement of a mistake; distinctions and contradistinctions are drawn; yet, thereby, they are not angered. It is thus, sire, that the learned converse.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: And how, revered sir, do kings converse?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: When kings are conversing, sire, they approve of some matter and order punishment for anyone who disagrees with that matter, saying: ‘Inflict a punishment on him.’ It is thus, sire, that kings converse.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: I, revered sir, will converse in the speech of the learned, not in the speech of kings. ... Let the revered one converse thus, let him not be afraid.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, is he who uprises the same or is he another?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Neither the same nor another. What do you think about this, sire? Now that you are grown up are you the same as you were when you were a boy, young, tender, lying on your back?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir. That boy, young, tender, lying on his back was one thing. I, who am now full-grown, am another.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: That being so, sire, you can have no mother, nor can you have a father... It is one ‘I’ that was the boy, young, tender, lying on his back and it is the same ‘I’ that am now full-grown, and all these are held together as a unity in dependence on this body itself.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Make a simile.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: It is as if, sire, some person might light a lamp. Would it burn all night long?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Yes, revered sir, it might burn all night long.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Is the flame of the first watch of the night the same as the flame of the middle watch?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Is the flame of the middle watch the same as the flame of the third watch?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Is it then, sire, that the lamp in the first watch was one thing, the lamp in the middle watch another, and the lamp in the third watch still another?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir, it was burning all through the night in dependence on itself.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Even so, sire, a continuity of phenomena is linked together. It uprises as one and ceases as another, linked together as though there were no before and no after. Hence it is neither the same nor another, but the subsequent consciousness is reckoned (together with) the preceding consciousness.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, who takes rebirth?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Mind-and-matter, sire, takes rebirth.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: What, is it this same mind-and-matter itself that takes rebirth?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: This same mind-and-matter does not itself take rebirth, sire; but, sire, by means of this mind-and-matter one does a good or bad deed and, because of this deed, another mind-and-matter takes rebirth.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: If, revered sir, this mind-and-matter itself does not take rebirth would one not be freed from evil deeds?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: If, sire, it did not take rebirth one would be freed from evil deeds. But because, sire, it takes rebirth one is not freed from evil deeds. ... Suppose, sire, some man were to steal another man’s mangoes and the owner of the mangoes were to seize him and bring him before the king... and he were to say, ‘Your majesty, I did not steal his mangoes; the mangoes he planted were different from these that I stole; I do not deserve punishment.’ Would he, sire, not deserve punishment?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Yes, revered sir, he would deserve punishment.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: For what reason?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Whatever he may say, the mangoes he stole resulted from the mangoes which, he admits, the other man planted.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Even so, sire, by means of this mind-and-matter one does a good or bad deed and, because of this deed, another mind-and-matter takes rebirth; therefore, one is not freed from evil deeds.

If the soul within sees a visible form through the eye just as we who are sitting here in the palace can look out of any window we want to look out of... can it not hear a sound, smell a smell, taste a taste, feel a touch and discriminate mental states through each of the other five doors besides the one you have specified in each case?

Thus too, would this soul within see visible forms more clearly when the doors of the eyes are removed? And if the ears were removed, the nose removed, the tongue removed, the body removed, would it hear a sound, smell a smell, taste a taste and feel a touch more clearly on account of the great space?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Thus these things are produced from a condition and there is no experiencer found here.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: If, sire, you walk at noon-time on the hot scorching ground, trampling on sharp grit, pebbles and sand, your feet will hurt you, your body will be tired, your mind will be disturbed and you will suffer bodily pain. Now, did you come on foot or in a vehicle?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: I, revered sir, did not come on foot. I came in a chariot.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: If, sire, you came in a chariot, show me the chariot. Is the pole the chariot, sire?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Is the axle the chariot?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Are the wheels the chariot?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Then, sire, are the pole, the axle, the wheels, the body, the flag-staff, the yoke, the reins, the goad all together the chariot?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Well then, sire, is the chariot apart from the pole, the axle, the wheels, the body, the flag-staff, the yoke, the reins and the goad?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, sire.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Sire, though I have been asking you repeatedly, I do not see this chariot. Chariot is only a sound. What then is the chariot you say you came in? You, sire, have spoken a falsehood, an untruth. There is no chariot.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: I am not, revered sir, speaking a lie. It is because of the pole, because of the axle, the wheels, the body, the flag-staff, the yoke, the reins and because of the goad that ‘chariot’ exists as a mere designation.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: It is good, sire, that you understand a chariot. Even so is it for me, sire, because of the hairs of the head … because of the urine, because of material form … because of consciousness, that ‘Nāgasena’ exists as a mere designation. However, in the ultimate sense there is no person as such that is found.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, will you converse with me?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: I will converse if you, sire, will converse in the speech of the learned, but if you converse in the speech of kings I will not converse.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: If, revered sir, this mind-and-matter itself does not take rebirth would one not be freed from evil deeds?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: If, sire, it did not take rebirth one would be freed from evil deeds. But because, sire, it takes rebirth one is not freed from evil deeds. ... Suppose, sire, some man were to steal another man’s mangoes and the owner of the mangoes were to seize him and bring him before the king... and he were to say, ‘Your majesty, I did not steal his mangoes; the mangoes he planted were different from these that I stole; I do not deserve punishment.’ Would he, sire, not deserve punishment?

turns.text: Yes, revered sir, he would deserve punishment.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: For what reason?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Whatever he may say, the mangoes he stole resulted from the mangoes which, he admits, the other man planted.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Even so, sire, by means of this mind-and-matter one does a good or bad deed and, because of this deed, another mind-and-matter takes rebirth; therefore, one is not freed from evil deeds.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing mark of faith?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Faith, sire, has tranquillizing as a distinguishing mark and also leaping forward as a distinguishing mark.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, how is tranquillizing a distinguishing mark of faith? Make a simile.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: As, sire, a Wheel-turning King going along a high road with his four limbed-army... might cross a small stretch of water and, as a result, that water will become foul, turbid and muddy. ... The king might have a water-clearing gem. So the men cast that water-clearing gem in the water. Immediately the various water plants disappear, the mud subsides and the water becomes clear, pure and serene. ... Sire, like the water is the mind... like the water-clearing gem is faith. ... Faith, as it is uprising, extirpates the hindrances...
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: And as you have spoken so eloquently of his nature, may I ask you further, Whether love is the love of something or of nothing?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Of something, surely.
turns.speaker: AGATHON

turns.text: Keep in mind what this is, and tell me what I want to know — whether Love desires that of which love is.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Yes, surely.
turns.speaker: AGATHON

turns.text: And does he possess, or does he not possess, that which he loves and desires?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Probably not, I should say.
turns.speaker: AGATHON

turns.text: Nay, replied Socrates, I would have you consider whether “necessarily” is not rather the word. The inference that he who desires something is in want of something, and that he who desires nothing is in want of nothing, is in my judgment, Agathon absolutely and necessarily true. What do you think?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: I agree with you.
turns.speaker: AGATHON

turns.text: Then Love wants and has not beauty?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Certainly.
turns.speaker: AGATHON

turns.text: And would you call that beautiful which wants and does not possess beauty?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Certainly not.
turns.speaker: AGATHON

turns.text: Then would you still say that love is beautiful?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: I fear that I did not understand what I was saying.
turns.speaker: AGATHON

turns.text: Well, Love is surely admitted by all to be a great god.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: By those who know or by those who do not know?
turns.speaker: DIOTIMA

turns.text: By all.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: And how, Socrates, can Love be acknowledged to be a great god by those who say that he is not a god at all?
turns.speaker: DIOTIMA

turns.text: And who are they?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: You and I are two of them.
turns.speaker: DIOTIMA

turns.text: How can that be?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: It is quite intelligible... you admitted that Love, because he was in want, desires those good and fair things of which he is in want? ... But how can he be a god who has no portion in what is either good or fair?
turns.speaker: DIOTIMA

turns.text: Impossible. What then is Love? Is he mortal?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: No... As in the former instance, he is neither mortal nor immortal, but in a mean between the two... He is a great spirit (daimon), and like all spirits he is intermediate between the divine and the mortal.
turns.speaker: DIOTIMA

turns.text: The truth of the matter is this: No god is a philosopher or seeker after wisdom, for he is wise already; nor does any man who is wise seek after wisdom. Neither do the ignorant seek after Wisdom. For herein is the evil of ignorance, that he who is neither good nor wise is nevertheless satisfied with himself: he has no desire for that of which he feels no want.
turns.speaker: DIOTIMA

turns.text: But — who then, Diotima, are the lovers of wisdom, if they are neither the wise nor the foolish?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: A child may answer that question; they are those who are in a mean between the two; Love is one of them. For wisdom is a most beautiful thing, and Love is of the beautiful; and therefore Love is also a philosopher: or lover of wisdom, and being a lover of wisdom is in a mean between the wise and the ignorant.
turns.speaker: DIOTIMA

turns.text: I mean to say, that all men are bringing to the birth in their bodies and in their souls... Beauty, then, is the destiny or goddess of parturition who presides at birth, and therefore, when approaching beauty, the conceiving power is propitious... and begets and bears fruit: at the sight of ugliness she frowns and contracts... For love, Socrates, is not, as you imagine, the love of the beautiful only.
turns.speaker: DIOTIMA

turns.text: What then?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: The love of generation and of birth in beauty.
turns.speaker: DIOTIMA

turns.text: Yes.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: But why of generation? Because to the mortal creature, generation is a sort of eternity and immortality... all men will necessarily desire immortality together with good: Wherefore love is of immortality.
turns.speaker: DIOTIMA

turns.text: He who would proceed aright in this matter should begin in youth to visit beautiful forms... soon he will of himself perceive that the beauty of one form is akin to the beauty of another... and will become a lover of all beautiful forms; in the next stage he will consider that the beauty of the mind is more honourable than the beauty of the outward form.
turns.speaker: DIOTIMA

turns.text: Until he is compelled to contemplate and see the beauty of institutions and laws... and after laws and institutions he will go on to the sciences, that he may see their beauty... until on that shore he grows and waxes strong, and at last the vision is revealed to him of a single science, which is the science of beauty everywhere.
turns.speaker: DIOTIMA

turns.text: He who has been instructed thus far... will suddenly perceive a nature of wondrous beauty... beauty absolute, separate, simple, and everlasting... This, my dear Socrates, is that life above all others which man should live.
turns.speaker: DIOTIMA

turns.text: I say, that he is exactly like the busts of Silenus... which are made to open in the middle, and have images of gods inside them. I say also that he is like Marsyas the satyr. You yourself will not deny, Socrates, that your face is like that of a satyr.
turns.speaker: ALCIBIADES

turns.text: But you produce the same effect with your words only... the mere fragments of you and your words, even at second-hand, and however imperfectly repeated, amaze and possess the souls of every man, woman, and child who comes within hearing of them.
turns.speaker: ALCIBIADES

turns.text: And if I were not afraid that you would think me hopelessly drunk, I would have sworn as well as spoken to the influence which they have always had and still have over me. For my heart leaps within me more than that of any Corybantian reveller, and my eyes rain tears when I hear them.
turns.speaker: ALCIBIADES

turns.text: I come to lay at your feet all that I have... in the hope that you will assist me in the way of virtue... I should certainly have more reason to be ashamed of what wise men would say if I were to refuse a favour to such as you.
turns.speaker: ALCIBIADES

turns.text: Alcibiades, my friend, you have indeed an elevated aim if what you say is true, and if there really is in me any power by which you may become better; truly you must see in me some rare beauty of a kind infinitely higher than any which I see in you.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: And therefore, if you mean to share with me and to exchange beauty for beauty, you will have greatly the advantage of me; you will gain true beauty in return for appearance — like Diomede, gold in exchange for brass. But look again, sweet friend, and see whether you are not deceived in me.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: That 'I may touch you,' he said, 'and have the benefit of that wise thought which came into your mind in the portico...'
turns.speaker: AGATHON

turns.text: How I wish, said Socrates, taking his place as he was desired, that wisdom could be infused by touch, out of the fuller the emptier man, as water runs through wool out of a fuller cup into an emptier one; if that were so, how greatly should I value the privilege of reclining at your side!
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: For you would have filled me full with a stream of wisdom plenteous and fair; whereas my own is of a very mean and questionable sort, no better than a dream.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: I can never sit on a platform and talk. It is too artificial. It is a waste of time to sit and discuss things in hypothetical or abstract terms. An angry man does not sit and talk and converse pleasantly about anger; he is too angry. So don't tell me that you are in crisis, that you are angry. Why talk of anger? You live and die in the hope that someday, somehow, you will no longer be angry. You are burdened with hope, and if this life seems hopeless, you invent the next life. There are no lives to come.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: Well, it certainly cannot be said that your talking gives hope to anyone. Why do you talk if not to console or instruct?
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: What am I to do? You come, I talk. Do you want me to criticize you, to throw stones? It is useless, for you are affected by nothing, having erected an impenetrable armor around yourself. You feel nothing. Unable to understand your situation, you react through thought, which is your ideas and mentations. Reaction is thought.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: But surely your sitting here and talking hour after hour indicates that you have a philosophy, a message to give, even if it is poorly understood by your listeners.
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: Not at all. There is nobody here talking, giving advice, feeling pain, or experiencing anything at all. Like a ball thrown against the wall, it bounces back, that is all. My talking is the direct result of your question, I have nothing here of my own, no obvious or hidden agenda, no product to sell, no axe to grind, nothing to prove.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: You have mercilessly cut off every possibility of rehabilitation, obliterating even the faint hope of escaping this unhappiness. There seems to be nothing left but self-destruction. Why not suicide?
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: If you commit suicide, it does not help the situation in any way. The moment after suicide the body begins to decay, returning back to other, differently organized forms of life, putting an end to nothing. Life has no beginning and no end. A dead and dying body feeds the hungry ants there in the grave, and rotting corpses give off soil-enriching chemicals, which in turn nourish other life forms. You cannot put an end to your life, it is impossible.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: The body is immortal and never asks silly questions like, "Is there immortality?" It knows that it will come to an end in that particular form, only to continue on in others. Questions about life after death are always asked out of fear.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: But for many of us life is a sacred thing. We struggle to protect our children, the environment, to avert another war ....
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: You are all neurotic people. You talk against birth control, drone on and on about the preciousness of life, then bomb and massacre. It is too absurd. You are concerned with an unborn life while you are killing thousands and thousands of people by bombing, starvation, poverty and terrorism. Your "concern" about life is only to make a political issue out of it. It is just an academic discussion. I am not interested in that.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: Yes, but many of us see all this and nevertheless are interested in changing things. It is not just egoism on our parts.
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: Are you really interested? Are you interested in the future of mankind? Your expressions of anger, righteousness, and caring have no meaning to me. It is just a ritual. You sit and talk, that's all. You are not at all angry. If you were angry at this moment, you would not ask this question, even to yourself. You sit everlastingly talking of anger. The angry wouldn't talk about it.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: So we must become aware of death, making it an object of our meditations, and treating it in such a romantic, mystical way. Is that it?
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: To describe that state as a meditative state full of awareness is romantic hogwash. Awareness! What a fantastic gimmick used to fool themselves and others. You can't be aware of every step, you only become self-conscious and awkward if you do. I once knew a man who was a harbor pilot. He had been reading about "passive awareness" and attempted to put it into practice. He, for the first time, nearly wrecked the ship he was guiding. Walking is automatic, and if you try to be aware of every step, you will go crazy. So don't invent meditative steps.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: It is the act of a person free from self-absorption, neurotic episodes, and self-pity. Is there any way to teach this? Can people be educated to be sane?
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: I don't believe in education. You can teach a technique -- mathematics, auto mechanics, but not integrity. How can you teach them about non-greed and non-ambition in an insanely greedy and ambitious society? You will only succeed in making them more neurotic. Look; you are a cheat. Your religious ambitions are just like the businessman's there. If you can't cheat there is something wrong. How do you think the rich man there got his great wealth? Through lectures about non-greed and selflessness? Not at all. He got it by cheating somebody.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: It is the guilt you have that compels you to talk of non-greed while you continue on with your greedy life. Your non-greed is invented by thought to keep you from facing the fact that greed is all that is there.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: Then why do you talk at all?
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: There is no particular charm in being antisocial. I don't give people what they want. When they realize they will not get what they want here, they invariably go away. ... When people come to talk they find themselves confronted with silence itself. That is why everybody who comes is automatically silent thereafter. If he cannot stand the silence and insists upon talking and discussing things, he will be forced to disagree and walk out. But if you stay long, you will be silenced, not because it is over-persuasive, more rational than you are, but because it is silence itself silencing that movement there. That silence burns everything here.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: How does intelligence fit into all this? You seem to indicate that there is a native intelligence that has nothing to do with the accumulation of knowledge and technique.
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: Accepting the limitations is intelligence. You are trying to free yourself from these natural limitations and that is the cause of your sorrow and pain. Your actions are such that one action limits the next action. Your action at this moment is limiting the next action. This action is a reaction. the question of freedom of action does not even arise. Therefore no fatalistic philosophy is needed. The word "karma" means an action without a reaction. ... Pure, spontaneous action free of all previous actions is meaningless. The one and only action is the response of this living organism to the stimuli around it.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: But still it seem to us that J. Krishnamurti, and perhaps a few others in history, have something to say. J. Krishnamurti appears to be what he claims he is, a free man.
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: He has something. I am fond of saying that he has SEEN the sugar cube, but has not TASTED the sugar cube. Whether that man, myself, or any other person is free or not is not your problem; it is the shibboleth of escapist minds, an amusement invented to avoid the real issue, which is your unfreedom. You may be sure of one thing; he who says he is a free man is a phoney.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: When these thoughts are not there, what is left is the simple, harmonious physical functioning of the organism. I am able to describe the way this organism is functioning because your question has created the challenge here. ... It functions in a state of not knowing. I never ask myself how I am functioning. I never question my actions, before, during, or after they occur. Does a computer ask how it is functioning?
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: But computers have no feeling, no psyche, no spiritual dimension. How can you compare ...?
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: You can't fit me into that religious framework. Any attempt on your part to translate what I am saying into your religious framework is to miss the point. I am not one of your holy men who say, "I am hanging, so come hang with me." All that stuff is a form of madness.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: Philosophers are often heard talking of a "now", independent of past and future. Is there such a thing as an eternal present?
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: The demand for more and more experience constitutes your "present", which is born out of the past. Look. Here is a microphone before you. You are looking at it. Is it possible for you to look at it without the word "Microphone"? The instrument you are using to look at and experience the microphone is the past, your past. If that is seen there is no future at all.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: When the past is not in operation there is no "present" at all, for what you are calling the "present" is the past repeating itself. In an actual state of "here and now" there is no past in operation and, therefore, no future.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: Is there any higher goal at all?
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: The so-called "highest goal" is like the horizon. The further you move towards it, the further it recedes. The goal, like the horizon, is not really there. It is a projection of your own fear and it moves away from you as you pursue it. How can you keep up with it? There is nothing that you can do. Still, it is desire that keeps you moving; no matter in which direction you move, it is the same.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: You are ruthlessly condemning whatever people have said so far. You may, in time, also be condemned and blasted for what you are saying.
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: If you have the guts, I will be the very first to salute you. But you must not rely on your holy books -- the Bhagavad Gita or Upanishads. You must challenge what I am saying without the help of your so-called authorities. You just don't have the guts to do that because you are relying upon the Gita, not upon yourself. That is why you will never be able to do it. If you have that courage, you are the only person who can falsify what I am saying.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: You prefer to toy with things, asking absurd questions like, "What happens to my body after death? Will the body be strong enough to take it?"
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: What the hell are you talking about? You are asking me what will happen to you if you touch that live electrical wire there. That is the kind of pointless question you are asking. You are not really interested at all. Perhaps after touching this you will be completely burnt and have to be thrown away. Perhaps others will get a shock themselves upon touching you, and you will become an untouchable! Look at what is implied by what I am saying. If you have the courage to touch life for the first time, you will never know what hit you.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: You don't stop searching because such an act would be the end of you. You are lost in a jungle, and you have no way of finding your way out. Night is fast approaching, the wild animals are there, including the cobras, and still you are lost. What do you do in such a situation? You just stop. You don't move....
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: But we can never be absolutely sure that there is not some way out, no matter how fantastic or improbable it may be ...
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: As long as there is that hope that you can somehow or the other get out of the jungle, so long will you continue what you are doing--searching--and so long you feel lost. You are lost only because you are searching. You have no way of finding your way out of the jungle.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: But if thought can create matter, how do you explain phenomena like Sai Baba producing watches out of thin air?
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: It's just not possible. Sai Baba is a magician. He used to produce Swiss watches. But after the Indian government placed an import tax on Swiss watches, he soon began producing Indian-made watches. I saw a man on television the other day, who could make a jet aircraft disappear before your very eyes! Sai Baba conjures up a watch. He gives it to an honored disciple, but he, Sai Baba, receives all the acclaim and applause. It all looks legitimate, but is only a gimmick. I make fun of such things. How can you take them seriously?
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: Yes, but what are you interested in? What makes you want to carry on living?
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: Whatever is there. Whatever is happening at the moment is all that there is for me.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: Come on. You're a here-and-now person, is that it?
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: No. To explain it that way is very misleading. I don't know how to explain it. Look, I read science-fiction books. Why? Because there is action there. I am not interested in the outcome at all, only the ongoing action. It is like a striptease. It is the stripping I find interesting, not the ending. Who cares about endings? Similarly, all your yesterdays, all your knowledge, and your very sense of self are dead things of the past. ... I am only interested in what is actually happening now, not tomorrow or yesterday.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: All this implies that we can never touch the same place at the same time and place. It is like two tape recording machines in a room playing old tapes to each other. You have no way of communicating anything to anybody. There is no communication at all. And when this is understood very clearly there is no need for communication at all.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: Which means that man's attempt to predict or preempt the future is condemned from the start, does it not? All this talk of communicating information, sharing knowledge, and interfacing is sheer bunk?
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: Yes, it is.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: Suppose I am serious about it and somehow find out....
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: No suppositions, please! What happened to me was acausal; it just happened. In spite of all my efforts, struggles, and intentions, this thing happened to me, and that is the miracle of miracles. You cannot make this happen. ... It is not an experience at all, and, therefore, cannot be communicated or transmitted. It is not something you share. It is a rare bird, that's all. All you can do is to put it in a museum and look at it, but you can never duplicate or share it.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: Look, I tried everything to find an answer to my burning obsession: "Is there such a thing as enlightenment at all, or have we all been fooled by abstractions?" That utter frustration and complete failure to answer that question created an intensity. ... I found out for myself that it was all bogus, there was nothing to it at all. ... Then one day the futility of what I was doing dawned upon me, and the question which had obsessed me for almost my entire life got burnt, then disappeared. After that there were no more questions. The thirst burned itself out without ever satisfying itself. Not answers, but the ending of questions, is the important thing.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: As scientists we want to find out if there is a uniqueness behind the apparent similarities in people. ... The yogins and religious leaders seem to offer us cases of really exceptional and unique persons. We want to study them, and you.
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: Don't you have any other way of finding out than going to these yogins...? The second-raters may submit to your scrutiny, but the real McCoy, if there is one, will never submit to your tests.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: That is the whole point: we are trying to find a way to test their credibility on a scientific basis.
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: I am afraid that you are making a horrendous mistake by even toying with the idea of giving any consideration to the claims that these people make.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: The only thing we have to work with is the statistics and data of what we call "normalcy", nothing more.
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: Your constant interpretation of data means that you are involved in what you are studying... I like to use the example of Newtonian physics. Within the Newtonian framework, things work in a certain way. Another scientist eventually comes along who is able to drop the Newtonian assumptions and thereby is able to perceive a whole new dimension of physics. Just as Newtonian principles eventually became a strait-jacket strangling creative thought, so your data about human uniqueness bars your looking at things, including yourself, anew.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: Listening to you now seems also to create problems for me.
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: You say you are listening. Even as I speak you are not listening to anything. You are not listening to me, but only to your own thoughts. ... I am not a fool.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: It is not so obvious to me that I am not listening to you. I seem to be listening to you and thinking about it simultaneously. Isn't this possible?
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: It is impossible. There is only one action possible for you: thinking. ... Thought creates the space between the thinker and his thoughts, and then tells himself, "I am looking at my thoughts." Is it possible? ... try to look at your thoughts at this very moment. I am asking you to do something which is quite simple.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: If you will tell me how to look at thought, I will be your student.
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: If you repeat a mantra, that is thought. The repetition of the mantra is another thought. The idea that these repetitive thoughts have not succeeded... is another thought. What is thought other than this? I want to know.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: You will never be free from selfishness.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: But all the saints, saviors and religions of all times have encouraged us to be unselfish... It must therefore be possible.
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: Because it is crystal clear to me that you have invented this idea of selflessness to protect yourself from the actual -- your selfishness. ... Look at it this way; it is like the horizon. Actually, there is no horizon. The more you move towards the horizon, the more it moves away. ... Likewise, there is no such thing as selflessness at all.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: Yes, but what about those who are not searching for some illusory abstraction, but simply happiness?
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: Their search for happiness is no different from the spiritual pursuit. It is the pursuit of pleasure, spirituality being the greatest, ultimate pleasure.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: So this pursuit has to go?
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: Don't say it should go. Wanting selfishness to go is part and parcel of the selfish pursuit of a more pleasurable state -- selflessness. Both do not exist. That is why you are eternally unhappy.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: But the key question remains: how is one not to want?
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: Again you ask "how", thus avoiding the issue. There is no "how" at all. "How" is the trickiest question, for in asking it you are doomed. ... That is the one question which has transformed itself into millions of questions.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: Brushing aside the question of how to be free from constant wanting, it seems obvious from what you have said that one must be free first from the influence of the past, or one's memory.
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: If you go on trying to suppress the past, trying to live in what you call "the present", you will drive yourself crazy. ... If you try to control the natural flow of the river through all these artificial means--building a dam so to speak--you will inundate and destroy the whole thing. That is why you find thoughts welling up inside you despite your efforts to control...
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: How does this process of accumulation work?
turns.speaker: Q

turns.text: The only way the self can add more and more knowledge and experience is to endlessly ask itself the meaningless question "How? How am I to live?" ... You are merely asking for the same kind of knowledge.
turns.speaker: U.G.

turns.text: Are you recognizing mind essence?
turns.speaker: Rinpoche

turns.text: It's difficult; it is very short.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: What's the trouble you're experiencing? What is the difficulty, exacdy? If it's very short, what is the problem in repeating it many times?
turns.speaker: Rinpoche

turns.text: Is this short moment something you create by meditating?
turns.speaker: Rinpoche

turns.text: No.
turns.speaker: Student

turns.text: Then it's not really difficult, is it? If you want the moment to last a long time, and you want to immediately become an arhat, then you can say it is very difficult.
turns.speaker: Rinpoche

turns.text: From beginningless lifetimes until now we have been deluded. To accomplish great achievements in the span of five or six years is difficult, because we have such a deeply ingrown habit of fixation and delusion.
turns.speaker: Rinpoche

turns.text: Now we need to attain a new habit - not by meditating on an it, but by growing accustomed to this recognition.
turns.speaker: Rinpoche

turns.text: Right now this recognition of mind essence is like a small infant, whereas the deluded thinking is like a strong person, a grown-up who takes this infant on its back and runs around everywhere.
turns.speaker: Rinpoche

turns.text: The small infant appears to be powerless. Our rigpa right now is like infant rigpa.
turns.speaker: Rinpoche

turns.text: What mantra are you using?
turns.speaker: Sakya Pandita

turns.text: OM BENZA CHILI CHILAYA SARVA BIGHANAN BAM HUNG PHAT.
turns.speaker: Meditator

turns.text: Oh, no! That's the wrong mantra; it's supposed to begin with OM BENZA KILl KILAYA. That's where the real meaning lies, in the words: 'Vajra Kilaya with consort, the Ten Sons and all the Eaters and Slayers.' They are contained within the sounds of the mantra.
turns.speaker: Sakya Pandita

turns.text: No, no, the words are not as important as the state of mind. Pure mind is more important than pure sound. I said CHILI CHILAYA in the past and that's what I will continue to say in the future. No doubt about that! You, on the other hand, will need my phurba.
turns.speaker: Meditator

turns.text: And the meditator gave Sakya Pandita his kilaya dagger, saying, "You take this with you."
turns.speaker: Rinpoche (Narrator)

turns.text: It becomes like the guy who visualized himself as Yamantaka and couldn't get out the entrance of his cave because his horns were too big.
turns.speaker: Rinpoche (Narrator)

turns.text: [The guru called for him to come]
turns.speaker: Guru

turns.text: Sorry! I can't come out! My horns get stuck in the doorway.
turns.speaker: Student (Yamantaka)

turns.text: What mantra are you using?
turns.speaker: Sakya Pandita

turns.text: OM BENZA CHILI CHILAYA SARVA BIGHANAN BAM HUNG PHAT.
turns.speaker: Meditator

turns.text: Oh, no! That's the wrong mantra; it's supposed to begin with OM BENZA KILl KILAYA. That's where the real meaning lies, in the words: 'Vajra Kilaya with consort, the Ten Sons and all the Eaters and Slayers.' They are contained within the sounds of the mantra.
turns.speaker: Sakya Pandita

turns.text: No, no, the words are not as important as the state of mind. Pure mind is more important than pure sound. I said CHILI CHILAYA in the past and that's what I will continue to say in the future. No doubt about that! You, on the other hand, will need my phurba.
turns.speaker: Meditator

turns.text: And the meditator gave Sakya Pandita his kilaya dagger, saying, "You take this with you."
turns.speaker: Rinpoche (Narrator)

turns.text: In the seen will be only the seen; in the heard will be only the heard; in the sensed will be only the sensed; in the cognized will be only the cognized.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: When for you there will be only the seen in the seen, only the heard in the heard, only the sensed in the sensed, only the cognized in the cognized, then there is no you in connection with that.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: When there is no you in connection with that, there is no you there. When there is no you there, you are neither here nor yonder nor between the two. This, just this, is the end of stress.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: A person has six properties: the earth property, the liquid property, the fire property, the wind property, the space property, and the consciousness property.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: And what is the earth property? Anything internal, within oneself, that's hard, solid, & sustained: head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, tendons, bones… this is called the internal earth property.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: Now both the internal earth property and the external earth property are simply earth property. And that should be seen as it actually is present with right discernment: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: When one sees it thus as it actually is present with right discernment, one becomes disenchanted with the earth property and makes the earth property fade from the mind.
turns.speaker: THE BUDDHA

turns.text: This infinite and eternal self of mine, how am I to know it?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: The self you want to know, is it some second self? Are you made of several selves? Surely, there is only one self and you are that self. The self you are is the only self there is. Remove and abandon your wrong ideas about yourself and there it is, in all its glory. It is only your mind that prevents self-knowledge.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: How am I to be rid of the mind? And is life without mind at all possible on the human level?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: There is no such thing as mind. There are ideas and some of them are wrong. Abandon the wrong ideas, for they are false and obstruct your vision of yourself.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Which ideas are wrong and which are true?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Assertions are usually wrong and denials -- right.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: One cannot live by denying everything!
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Only by denying can one live. Assertion is bondage. To question and deny is necessary. It is the essence of revolt and without revolt there can be no freedom. There is no second, or higher self to search for. You are the highest self, only give up the false ideas you have about your self. Both faith and reason tell you that you are neither the body, nor its desires and fears, nor are you the mind with its fanciful ideas, nor the role society compels you to play, the person you are supposed to be. Give up the false and the true will come into its own. You say you want to know your self. You are your self -- you cannot be anything but what you are. Is knowing separate from being? Whatever you can know with your mind is of the mind, not you; about yourself you can only say: 'I am, I am aware, I like It'.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: I find being alive a painful state.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: You cannot be alive for you are life itself. It is the person you imagine yourself to be that suffers, not you. Dissolve it in awareness. It is merely a bundle of memories and habits. From the awareness of the unreal to the awareness of your real nature there is a chasm which you will easily cross, once you have mastered the art of pure awareness.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: All I know is that I do not know myself.
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: How do you know, that you do not know your self? Your direct insight tells you that yourself you know first, for nothing exists to you without your being there to experience its existence. You imagine you do not know your self, because you cannot describe your self. You can always say: 'I know that I am' and you will refuse as untrue the statement: 'I am not'. But whatever can be described cannot be your self, and what you are cannot be described. You can only know your self by being yourself without any attempt at self-definition and self-description. Once you have understood that you are nothing perceivable or conceivable, that whatever appears in the field of consciousness cannot be your self, you will apply yourself to the eradication of all self-identification, as the only way that can take you to a deeper realisation of your self. You literally progress by rejection -- a veritable rocket. To know that you are neither in the body nor in the mind, though aware of both, is already self-knowledge.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: If I am neither the body nor mind, how am I aware of them? How can I perceive something quite foreign to myself?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: 'Nothing is me,' is the first step. 'Everything is me' is the next. Both hang on the idea: 'there is a world'. When this too is given up, you remain what you are -- the non-dual Self. You are it here and now, but your vision is obstructed by your false ideas about your self.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: What is the cause of desire and fear?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Obviously, the memory of past pains and pleasures. There is no great mystery about it. Conflict arises only when desire and fear refer to the same object.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: How to put an end to memory?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: It is neither necessary, nor possible. realise that all happens in consciousness and you are the root, the source, the foundation of consciousness. The world is but a succession of experiences and you are what makes them conscious, and yet remain beyond all experience. It is like the heat, the flame and the burning wood. The heat maintains the flame, the flame consumes the wood. Without heat there would be neither flame nor fuel. Similarly, without awareness there would be no consciousness, nor life, which transforms matter into a vehicle of consciousness.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: You maintain that without me there would be no world, and that the world and my knowledge of the world are identical. Science has come to a quite different conclusion: the world exists as something concrete and continuous, while I am a by-product of biological evolution of the nervous system, which is primarily not so much a seat of consciousness, as a mechanism of survival as individual and species. Yours is altogether a subjective view, while science tries to describe everything in objective terms. Is this contradiction inevitable?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: The confusion is apparent and purely verbal. What is, is. It is neither subjective nor objective. Matter and mind are not separate, they are aspects of one energy. Look at the mind as a function of matter and you have science; look at matter as the product of the mind and you have religion.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: But what is true? What comes first, mind or matter?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Neither comes first. for neither appears alone. Matter is the shape, mind is the name. Together they make the world. Pervading and transcending is Reality, pure being -- awareness -- bliss, your very essence.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: What does it mean, nothing is? Do you turn blank, or go to sleep? Or do you dissolve the world and keep us all in abeyance, until we are brought back to life at the next flicker of your thought?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Oh, no, it is not that bad. The world of mind and matter, of names and shapes, continues, but it does not matter to me at all. It is like having a shadow. It is there -- following me wherever I go, but not hindering me in any way. It remains a world of experiences, but not of names and forms related to me by desires and fears. The experiences are qualityless, pure experiences, if I may say so. I call them experiences for the lack of a better word. They are like the waves on the surface of the ocean, the ever-present, but not affecting its peaceful power.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: You mean to say an experience can be nameless, formless, undefined?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: In the beginning all experience is such. It is only desire and fear, born of memory, that give it name and form and separate it from other experiences. It is not a conscious experience, for it is not in opposition to other experiences, yet it is an experience all the same.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: If it is not conscious, why talk about it?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Most of your experiences are unconscious. The conscious ones are very few. You are unaware of the fact because to you only the conscious ones count. Become aware of the unconscious .
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Can one be aware of the unconscious? How is it done?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Desire and fear are the obscuring and distorting factors. When mind is free of them the unconscious becomes accessible.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Does it mean that the unconscious becomes conscious?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: It is rather the other way round. The conscious becomes one with the unconscious. The distinction ceases, whichever way you look at it.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: I am puzzled. How can one be aware and yet unconscious?
turns.speaker: Questioner

turns.text: Awareness is not limited to consciousness. It is of all that is. Consciousness is of duality. There is no duality in awareness. It is one single block of pure cognition. In the same way one can talk of the pure being and pure creation -- nameless, formless, silent and yet absolutely real, powerful, effective. Their being indescribable does not affect them in the least. While they are unconscious, they are essential. The conscious cannot change fundamentally, it can only modify. Any thing, to change, must pass through death, through obscuration and dissolution. Gold jewellery must be melted down before it is cast into another shape. What refuses to die cannot be reborn.
turns.speaker: Maharaj

turns.text: Yogic texts talk about prana flowing through 72,000 nadis, with Ida, Pingala and Sushumna as the main channels. Is that an actual subtle energy system in the body, or basically poetic metaphor for nerves and breathing?

At least you didn’t say ‘quantum prana’, so we’re already above Instagram guru level. You’ve still fused three questions: is prana a physical energy, are nadis literal tubes, and does any of this track measurable physiology or is it just story. Until we pry those apart, “real or metaphor” is you begging the universe for a yes/no sticker on a badly posed sentence.

Alright, so split those layers. What’s text-level myth, what’s reproducible subjective experience, and what’s actually happening physiologically when someone does ‘move prana through the nadis’ practices?

Text level: late Upanishads and Haṭha texts trot out 72,000 nadis and three primaries as a practice map and liberation story, not as a lab manual. Experiential level: people who do pranayama, bandhas and visualisation long enough report fairly stereotyped ‘currents’, ‘heat’ and midline or lateral flows that slot neatly into the Ida–Pingala–Sushumna template. Physiology level: slow, controlled breathing and postural locks reliably shift autonomic balance, heart-rate variability and brain rhythms—but no scan has ever labelled a voxel ‘Ida nadi’ (Jerath2006; Zaccaro2018).

So concretely: if we cut or scan a body we don’t find ‘Ida’ and ‘Pingala’ as separate structures, but techniques framed as moving prana still ride on real autonomic and interoceptive shifts that people then describe as currents. Is that accurate, or am I just repainting everything as Western physiology cosplay?

You’re mostly right, with one line you don’t get to blur. We do have robust data on slow breathing changing HRV, blood pressure oscillations and brain rhythms; we do not have anatomical or imaging evidence for a distinct nadi network on top of nerves, vessels and fascia (Jerath2006; Zaccaro2018). So yes, practices do something real, and yes, practitioners feel that as flows. The second you claim ‘and therefore the 72,000 channels literally exist as subtle plumbing’, you’ve left integration and walked into fanfic with a stethoscope.

So the honest position is something like: pranayama and nadi work are real levers on breathing, autonomic tone and interoception that traditions narrate as prana flows—but that doesn’t cash out as a literal extra plumbing system. I still feel like reducing it all to HRV misses why the prana model is practically sticky.

Good, that itch is the part of you that knows ‘being regulated’ isn’t the whole point of a spiritual technology. You now have: a map-level construct that shapes how people aim attention and effort (the prana–nadi schema), concrete biological mechanisms for slow-breathing effects, and clear limits where the evidence stops (Jerath2006; Zaccaro2018). Now answer your own question without flinching: in that frame, what does it actually mean to say ‘Ida and Pingala are real’ without LARPing as a Victorian anatomist or napalming the subtle-body language as worthless?

I’d say: prana and the nadis are ‘real’ as a disciplined way of organising breath, attention and felt-body experience that plugs into real autonomic and cardiorespiratory mechanisms we can measure. Slow, structured breathing and related techniques shift vagal tone, HRV and interoception; practitioners experience and train those shifts as flows along Ida, Pingala or Sushumna. The 72,000 figure and the subtle plumbing story aren’t supported as literal anatomy or new physics, but the map still does real work as a phenomenological and ritual technology, so I don’t have to pretend it’s biology and I don’t have to throw it out as useless myth either.

That’s the adult position: keep the map as a practice-effective way of sculpting experience, tie what you can to autonomic and respiratory mechanisms, and park the ‘extra invisible tubing’ and ‘mystical energy field’ parts in the metaphysics penalty box (Jerath2006; Zaccaro2018). You moved from ‘is there a hidden energy system?’ to ‘this is a symbolic-phenomenological framework riding on known physiology, with unproven ontological add-ons clearly marked as such’. You don’t need me for this one anymore.

Hermetic texts map planets to metals and human traits — like Mars to iron and aggression. Is there any hard evidence that things like trace minerals or circadian cycles tied to planetary motion actually create these temperament patterns, or is that all just symbolic poetry people are over-reading?

You’ve glued three different things together and asked if the universe secretly agrees with your vibe chart: Hermetic symbolism, blood chemistry, and orbital mechanics. Before we go hunting for a ‘Mars in your hemoglobin’ effect, we need to separate: what the correspondences were for, what biology actually does, and how much causal bandwidth planets have on your nervous system. Right now you’re asking if a metaphor is doing biochemical work.

Okay, so treat the grid as symbolic first. But at the same time: iron levels clearly affect energy and mood, circadian cycles obviously shape behavior, and we do live inside a gravitational and electromagnetic environment. I’m trying to see if there’s any principled overlap, not just ‘Mars beams rage into you’. Where are the real frameworks that even could overlap with the Hermetic ones?

Good, now you’re asking ‘what could possibly be real here?’ instead of ‘did Mars invent my anger’.
On the biology side you’ve got: trace elements and mood or cognition (iron, zinc, lithium), plus circadian systems entrained by light–dark and seasons (Czeisler1999; Roenneberg2012). On the Hermetic side you’ve got an analogical architecture where Mars, iron, blood, war, and anger are clustered as ‘hot, cutting, outward’ (Campion2008). The right question isn’t ‘did they predict ferritin assays’, it’s ‘do any of our actual mechanisms live in the same rough semantic neighborhood as their symbols?’

So mechanistically, what’s actually on the table? I can see iron deficiency killing energy, lithium flattening mania, and circadian misalignment wrecking mood. But do any of those line up in a way that would pick out the Hermetic clusters, or is the overlap just ‘everything affects everything’?

Mechanistically, the universe is boringly local and specific compared to Hermetic charts. Iron status modulates oxygen transport and neurotransmitter systems, which shifts capacity and sometimes irritability but doesn’t magically encode ‘Mars-like’ rage (Beard2003). Lithium alters intracellular signaling and gene expression in ways that stabilize mood across the board (Malhi2013). Circadian clocks follow the sun, not Mars retrograde (Czeisler1999; Roenneberg2012). The only real overlap is that humans later painted these blunt, multi-factorial levers with planetary archetypes.

What about the ‘aligned to celestial mechanics’ angle? People love to bring up lunar cycles and gravitational effects. Is there any serious evidence that planetary positions or trace cosmic cycles meaningfully imprint on temperament, or does it mostly stop at light–dark and seasons?

When you do the math, Mars has roughly the same gravitational pull on you as a truck a few streets over; it’s not sculpting your amygdala. The hard evidence tops out at local cycles: solar day, seasons, maybe some contested and tiny lunar effects on sleep or menstruation (Jones2013). Large-scale tests find no robust links between horoscope sign and personality or life outcomes (Dean2007; Carlson1985). So yes, your physiology is tuned to the sky—but mainly to the nearest fusion reactor, not to symbolic Mars–iron–rage alignments.

So if I put this together: Hermetic correspondences are analogical maps, not hidden biomedical theories. Modern biology shows that minerals and circadian rhythms absolutely shape mood and behavior, but through broad, dose-dependent mechanisms that don’t uniquely pick out ‘Mars-iron-aggression’ clusters. And celestial mechanics matter for us mostly as local solar and seasonal cycles, with at best tiny and contested lunar effects, not as planet-specific temperament scripts. So any ‘Mars-iron’ truth is metaphorical rhyme plus opportunistic cherry-picking, not a real causal law.

Exactly. The Hermetic table is a poetic macrocosm–microcosm operating system; our trace-mineral and chronobiology models are blunt physiological levers; and the actual sky influences you mainly via sunrise, not via Mars’ horoscope. Where they ‘match’ is at the level of human pattern-seeking: we notice that iron, blood, weapons, and anger all feel hot and cutting, then staple that bundle to a red planet and call it Mars. The mistake is to promote that rhyme to a physics claim instead of using it as a disciplined metaphor.

The Akashic Records are meant to be this cosmic database of everything that ever happens. With things like the holographic universe idea and quantum entanglement, is there actually any serious physics that could back that up, or is the Akashic stuff just mysticism with science words glued on?

You just stapled a theosophical clairvoyance myth, a black hole entropy principle and quantum entanglement into one Frankenstein theory and asked if it is real. First we separate: Akashic Records are a metaphysical claim about a readable cosmic diary; holography and entanglement are strict mathematical frameworks about information bounds and correlations. Until you stop treating all uses of the word information as the same thing, the question is noise, not inquiry.

Alright, so what are the main pieces here then? On one side Akashic Records as a kind of cosmic archive, and on the other holographic principle and entanglement as physics talking about information. How do those actually line up conceptually, if at all?

On the esoteric side you have Akashic Records as a symbolic and metaphysical field that somehow carries a readable history of everything. On the physics side, the holographic principle says the maximum information content of a region scales with its boundary area, and AdS or black hole models realize that as a duality, while entanglement gives nonclassical correlations that still obey no communication constraints. Those are different registers: one is a mythic map plus ontology claim, the others are formal statements about degrees of freedom, entropy and correlations.

Mechanistically then, could spacetime itself act like some kind of storage medium?
