turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: How, revered Nāgasena, do the learned converse?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: When the learned are conversing, sire, there is a turning over and an unravelling of the subject; then there is a refutation and an acknowledgement of a mistake; distinctions and contradistinctions are drawn; yet, thereby, they are not angered. It is thus, sire, that the learned converse.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: And how, revered sir, do kings converse?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: When kings are conversing, sire, they approve of some matter and order punishment for anyone who disagrees with that matter, saying: ‘Inflict a punishment on him.’ It is thus, sire, that kings converse.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: I, revered sir, will converse in the speech of the learned, not in the speech of kings. ... Let the revered one converse thus, let him not be afraid.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, is he who uprises the same or is he another?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Neither the same nor another. What do you think about this, sire? Now that you are grown up are you the same as you were when you were a boy, young, tender, lying on your back?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir. That boy, young, tender, lying on his back was one thing. I, who am now full-grown, am another.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: That being so, sire, you can have no mother, nor can you have a father... It is one ‘I’ that was the boy, young, tender, lying on his back and it is the same ‘I’ that am now full-grown, and all these are held together as a unity in dependence on this body itself.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Make a simile.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: It is as if, sire, some person might light a lamp. Would it burn all night long?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Yes, revered sir, it might burn all night long.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Is the flame of the first watch of the night the same as the flame of the middle watch?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Is the flame of the middle watch the same as the flame of the third watch?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Is it then, sire, that the lamp in the first watch was one thing, the lamp in the middle watch another, and the lamp in the third watch still another?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir, it was burning all through the night in dependence on itself.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Even so, sire, a continuity of phenomena is linked together. It uprises as one and ceases as another, linked together as though there were no before and no after. Hence it is neither the same nor another, but the subsequent consciousness is reckoned (together with) the preceding consciousness.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, who takes rebirth?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Mind-and-matter, sire, takes rebirth.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: What, is it this same mind-and-matter itself that takes rebirth?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: This same mind-and-matter does not itself take rebirth, sire; but, sire, by means of this mind-and-matter one does a good or bad deed and, because of this deed, another mind-and-matter takes rebirth.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: If, revered sir, this mind-and-matter itself does not take rebirth would one not be freed from evil deeds?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: If, sire, it did not take rebirth one would be freed from evil deeds. But because, sire, it takes rebirth one is not freed from evil deeds. ... Suppose, sire, some man were to steal another man’s mangoes and the owner of the mangoes were to seize him and bring him before the king... and he were to say, ‘Your majesty, I did not steal his mangoes; the mangoes he planted were different from these that I stole; I do not deserve punishment.’ Would he, sire, not deserve punishment?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Yes, revered sir, he would deserve punishment.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: For what reason?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Whatever he may say, the mangoes he stole resulted from the mangoes which, he admits, the other man planted.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Even so, sire, by means of this mind-and-matter one does a good or bad deed and, because of this deed, another mind-and-matter takes rebirth; therefore, one is not freed from evil deeds.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, is there such a thing as an experiencer?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: What does this ‘experiencer’ mean, sire?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: A soul within that sees a visible form with the eye, hears a sound with the ear... Just as we who are sitting here in the palace can look out of any window we want to look out of, even so, revered sir, this soul within can look out of any door it wants to look out of.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: I will talk to you, sire, about the five doors. Listen and attend carefully. If the soul within sees a visible form through the eye just as we who are sitting here in the palace can look out of any window we want to look out of... can it not hear a sound, smell a smell, taste a taste, feel a touch and discriminate mental states through each of the other five doors besides the one you have specified in each case?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Again, sire, we who are sitting here in the palace will see visible forms out there before us more clearly in the great space if these network windows are removed. Thus too, would this soul within see visible forms more clearly when the doors of the eyes are removed? And if the ears were removed, the nose removed, the tongue removed, the body removed, would it hear a sound, smell a smell, taste a taste and feel a touch more clearly on account of the great space?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Because, sire, of the eye and visible form eye-consciousness arises. ... Thus these things are produced from a condition and there is no experiencer found here.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, where eye-consciousness arises, does mind-consciousness also arise there?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Yes, sire, mind-consciousness also arises there.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Now, revered sir, does eye-consciousness instruct mind-consciousness, saying ‘Where I arise do you likewise arise,’ or does mind-consciousness instruct eye-consciousness, saying ‘Where you arise I will likewise arise’?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: No, sire, there is no conversation between them.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Then how is it, revered Nāgasena, that where eye-consciousness arises there mind-consciousness also arises?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: It is because of tendency, sire, because of door, because of habit and because of practice. ... When it is raining by what means may the water run away?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: It might run away by means of some slope.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: But, sire, if it continued to rain, by what means would that later amount of water run away?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: It would take the same course as the earlier water.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Then, sire, does the earlier water instruct the later, saying ‘You run away by the same course as I do,’ or does the later water instruct the earlier, saying ‘I will also run away by the same course as you will take’?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: No, revered sir, there is no conversation between them; they run away because there is a slope.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Even so, sire, it is because of tendency that where eye-consciousness arises, mind-consciousness arises there too.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, for whom is the greater demerit: he who does an evil deed knowingly or he who does an evil deed unknowingly?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: His is the greater demerit, sire, who does an evil deed unknowingly.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Well then, revered sir, do we doubly punish any of our family or our court who does an evil deed unknowingly?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: What do you think about this, sire? If a man should unknowingly take hold of a red-hot ball of iron, glowing with heat, and another should take hold of it knowingly, which would be more severely burnt?
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: He who took hold of it unknowingly, sire, would be more severely burnt.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Even so, sire, the greater demerit is his who does an evil deed unknowingly.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing mark of faith?
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: Faith, sire, has tranquillizing as a distinguishing mark and also leaping forward as a distinguishing mark.
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, how is tranquillizing a distinguishing mark of faith? Make a simile.
turns.speaker: King Milinda

turns.text: As, sire, a Wheel-turning King going along a high road with his four limbed-army... might cross a small stretch of water and, as a result, that water will become foul, turbid and muddy. ... The king might have a water-clearing gem. So the men cast that water-clearing gem in the water. Immediately the various water plants disappear, the mud subsides and the water becomes clear, pure and serene. ... Sire, like the water is the mind... like the water-clearing gem is faith. ... Faith, as it is uprising, extirpates the hindrances...
turns.speaker: Nāgasena

turns.text:
I will question the ascetic Gotama. If he answers me well, so much the better. If he does not, I will shake him, agitate him, pull him about, as a strong man might shake a feeble goat!

Form, Master Gotama, is the self. Feeling is the self. Perception is the self. Fabrications are the self. Consciousness is the self.

Exactly so, Master Gotama.

But what is your doctrine, Aggivessana? What is it that you hold?

Do you say, Aggivessana, that all five aggregates are the self?

fields.intent: Setting up the trap by forcing the student to explicitly commit to the full scope of their error.

turns.text:
Impermanent, Master Gotama.

Stressful, Master Gotama.

No indeed, Master Gotama.

Aggivessana, is form permanent or impermanent?

Is what is impermanent easeful or stressful?

Is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, stressful, subject to change, as ‘This is mine; this is my self; this is what I am’?

fields.intent: Forces the student to admit their original claim (Form is Self) is logically untenable given the admitted premises.

turns.text: I did, Master Gotama.

Aggivessana, did you not say that form is the self?

But now, Aggivessana, you admit it is impermanent, stressful, subject to change, and cannot rightly be regarded as self. How can both of your claims stand?

fields.intent: Explicitly stating the contradiction between the two accepted premises.

turns.text:
Master Gotama, let us set aside form. Let us discuss feeling...

But Master Gotama, I wish to proceed.

Then proceed, Master Gotama.

Aggivessana, we will not move on until we settle what has already been said.

Aggivessana, when you made your claim, you stood upon it. Now that it falters, you try to flee. But the matter must be resolved here.

fields.intent: Attacking the student's behavior (fleeing) as an inconsistency with their earlier confidence.

turns.text:
Impermanent, Master Gotama.

Impermanent, Master Gotama.

Impermanent, Master Gotama.

No indeed, Master Gotama.

Aggivessana, is feeling permanent or impermanent?

Is perception permanent or impermanent?

And fabrications, consciousness — are they permanent or impermanent?

Then, Aggivessana, is it fitting to regard any of these as ‘This is mine; this is my self; this is what I am’?

fields.intent: Finalizing the destruction of the self-view across all categories.

turns.text:
Lady, what is feeling?

But Lady, what is the cause and condition for feeling?

But Lady, what is the cause and condition for contact?

There are three feelings, friend Visakha: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

Contact, friend Visakha, is the cause and condition for feeling.

Name-and-form is the condition for contact.

fields.intent: Tracing the causal chain one step further back.

turns.text:
Lady, what is the cause and condition for craving?

And what is the cause and condition for feeling?

And for contact?

Feeling, friend Visakha, is the cause and condition for craving.

Contact is the condition for feeling.

Name-and-form is the condition for contact.

fields.intent: Reinforcing the base link.

turns.text:
Lady, what is the cessation of craving?

And what is the path leading to the cessation of craving?

And what is the Noble Eightfold Path?

The ending of craving, the abandonment of craving, the relinquishing of craving—this, friend Visakha, is the cessation of craving.

The Noble Eightfold Path leads to the cessation of craving.

fields.intent: Identifying the structural means (Path) to the end (Cessation).

turns.text:
Lady, what is the self? And what is not-self?

Lady, why are these not self?

Is there, then, any self?

Form, friend Visakha, is not self. Feeling is not self. Perception is not self. Fabrications are not self. Consciousness is not self.

Because, friend Visakha, they are impermanent, changing, subject to decay.

Visakha, that is a matter for the Tathāgata.

fields.intent: Refusing to speculate on the metaphysical 'is there' question, referring to authority/scope limits.

turns.text:
Lady, feeling is pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.

Contact is the cause of feeling.

But tell me now, friend Visakha—what is feeling?

And what is the cause of feeling?

Good, Visakha. You have understood well.

fields.intent: Confirming the success of the interaction.

turns.text:
Master Gotama, this is my view: ‘I take no view. Nothing is acceptable to me.’

Yes, Master Gotama, this is truly my view.

Master Gotama, it seems this view does not stand as I thought.

Aggivessana, do you hold that view as true?

But if you take that as true, then at least this one view is acceptable to you.

fields.intent: Revealing the self-refuting nature of 'no view is acceptable' (since that statement itself is accepted).

turns.text:
Master Gotama, how does this apply to one who claims that nothing is acceptable?

So even rejecting all things creates a bond?

Aggivessana, there are three kinds of views: ‘Everything is pleasing to me,’ ‘Nothing is pleasing to me,’ and ‘Some things are pleasing to me and some are not.’

One who says that nothing is acceptable is bound by that view, and thus is not free from clinging.

Indeed. To grasp the idea ‘nothing is acceptable’ is itself a form of clinging.

fields.intent: Showing that the rejection of views is itself a form of binding/clinging.

turns.text:
Impermanent, Master Gotama.

Impermanent, Master Gotama.

Impermanent as well.

Aggivessana, when you experience a pleasant feeling, is it permanent or impermanent?

And unpleasant feelings—permanent or impermanent?

Neutral feelings—permanent or impermanent?

fields.intent: Applying logic to the final category.

turns.text:
Master Gotama, how should one attend to such seeing?

So one stands apart from it?

Aggivessana, when one sees the arising of feeling, its passing away, and its change while it persists—then one is not bound by feeling.

Attend simply as ‘feeling arises, feeling remains, feeling passes away.’ When one sees this, there is no ‘I’ in feeling.

Just so. One stands as the watcher, not the owned.

fields.intent: Stabilizing the student in the witness position.

turns.text: Master Gotama, marvelous indeed are these teachings.
When views are abandoned, Aggivessana, one knows directly what arises and ceases.

fields.intent: Pointing to the direct knowledge that remains when views are gone.

turns.text:
Venerable sir, what is right view?

How does this duality bind the world?

Then right view avoids both?

Kaccana, by and large, this world is supported by a duality: by existence and by non-existence.

One who sees the arising of the world as it really is does not hold the view of non-existence. One who sees the cessation of the world as it really is does not hold the view of existence.

Indeed. Right view is free from these two extremes.

fields.intent: Establishing the 'Right View' as freedom from the binary.

turns.text:
What is the view that abandons clinging?

So right view is seeing conditions?

This seems a middle way beyond views.

Kaccana, this world is mostly bound by clinging, taking hold of something or other.

When one sees dependent origination as it is—‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises’—one does not cling to any view of existence or non-existence.

Just so. Seeing conditional arising and conditional cessation.

It is the middle by which the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma.

fields.intent: Validating the student's insight as the core method ('The Middle').

turns.text:
Venerable sir, how does one see rightly?

And seeing this, what does one abandon?

So the sense of self depends on misunderstanding the process?

By seeing that all is merely arising and ceasing.

One abandons the thought ‘I am’ in regard to these processes.

Just so. Where there is arising and ceasing, no self is found.

fields.intent: Confirming the direct insight that no self is found in the process.

turns.text:
Venerable sir, should one say ‘there is a self’?

Then should one say ‘there is no self’?

Then how should the matter be seen?

Kaccana, saying ‘there is a self’ is one extreme.

Saying ‘there is no self’ is the other extreme.

With right wisdom seeing only arising and ceasing.

fields.intent: Pointing back to the direct observation of process as the solution to the binary trap.

turns.text: I, revered sir, did not come on foot. I came in a chariot.

If, sire, you walk at noon-time on the hot scorching ground, trampling on sharp grit, pebbles and sand, your feet will hurt you, your body will be tired, your mind will be disturbed and you will suffer bodily pain. Now, did you come on foot or in a vehicle?

If, sire, you came in a chariot, show me the chariot. Is the pole the chariot, sire?

fields.intent: Begins the deconstruction process by isolating parts and asking if they are the whole.

turns.text: No, revered sir.
Is the axle the chariot?

fields.intent: Continues the iterative negation of parts.

turns.text: No, revered sir.
Are the wheels the chariot?

fields.intent: Continues the iterative negation of parts.

turns.text: No, revered sir.
Then, sire, are the pole, the axle, the wheels, the body, the flag-staff, the yoke, the reins, the goad all together the chariot?

fields.intent: Continues the iterative negation of parts.

turns.text: No, revered sir.
Well then, sire, is the chariot apart from the pole, the axle, the wheels, the body, the flag-staff, the yoke, the reins and the goad?

fields.intent: Tests if the mere heap of parts constitutes the essence.

turns.text: No, sire.

Sire, though I have been asking you repeatedly, I do not see this chariot. Chariot is only a sound. What then is the chariot you say you came in? You, sire, have spoken a falsehood, an untruth. There is no chariot.

fields.intent: Tests if the essence exists independently of the parts.

turns.text: I am not, revered sir, speaking a lie. It is because of the pole, because of the axle, the wheels, the body, the flag-staff, the yoke, the reins and because of the goad that ‘chariot’ exists as a mere designation.

It is good, sire, that you understand a chariot. Even so is it for me, sire, because of the hairs of the head … because of the urine, because of material form … because of consciousness, that ‘Nāgasena’ exists as a mere designation. However, in the ultimate sense there is no person as such that is found.

fields.intent: Reconstructs the understanding: just as 'chariot' is a label for parts, 'self' is a label for aggregates.

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, will you converse with me?
I will converse if you, sire, will converse in the speech of the learned, but if you converse in the speech of kings I will not converse.

fields.intent: Establishes the rules of the dialogue itself.

turns.text: How, revered Nāgasena, do the learned converse?

When the learned are conversing, sire, there is a turning over and an unravelling of the subject; then there is a refutation and an acknowledgement of a mistake; distinctions and contradistinctions are drawn; yet, thereby, they are not angered. It is thus, sire, that the learned converse.

fields.intent: Defines the dialectical method (refutation, no anger).

turns.text: And how, revered sir, do kings converse?

When kings are conversing, sire, they approve of some matter and order punishment for anyone who disagrees with that matter, saying: ‘Inflict a punishment on him.’ It is thus, sire, that kings converse.

fields.intent: Contrasts the previous definition with power-based discourse to force a choice.

turns.text: I, revered sir, will converse in the speech of the learned, not in the speech of kings. Let the revered one converse unreservedly as he converses with a monk or a novice or a lay follower or with a monastery attendant. Let the revered one converse thus, let him not be afraid.
Revered Nāgasena, is he who uprises the same or is he another?
Neither the same nor another. What do you think about this, sire? Now that you are grown up are you the same as you were when you were a boy, young, tender, lying on your back?

fields.intent: Rejects the binary choice (same/other) and introduces a continuity model via personal history.

turns.text: No, revered sir. That boy, young, tender, lying on his back was one thing. I, who am now full-grown, am another.

That being so, sire, you can have no mother, nor can you have a father... It is one ‘I’ that was the boy, young, tender, lying on his back and it is the same ‘I’ that am now full-grown, and all these are held together as a unity in dependence on this body itself.

fields.intent: Shows the absurd consequence of the King's 'different' view (no parents/teachers).

turns.text: Make a simile.
It is as if, sire, some person might light a lamp. Would it burn all night long?

fields.intent: Uses the lamp analogy to model process continuity without static substance.

turns.text: Yes, revered sir, it might burn all night long.
Is the flame of the first watch of the night the same as the flame of the middle watch?

fields.intent: Deconstructs the identity of the flame moments.

turns.text: No, revered sir.
Is the flame of the middle watch the same as the flame of the third watch?

fields.intent: Continuing the deconstruction.

turns.text: No, revered sir.
Is it then, sire, that the lamp in the first watch was one thing, the lamp in the middle watch another, and the lamp in the third watch still another?

fields.intent: Tests if the lack of identity implies total separation (three different lamps).

turns.text: No, revered sir, it was burning all through the night in dependence on itself.

Even so, sire, a continuity of phenomena is linked together. It uprises as one and ceases as another, linked together as though there were no before and no after. Hence it is neither the same nor another, but the subsequent consciousness is reckoned (together with) the preceding consciousness.

fields.intent: Formalizes the 'continuity' model: dependence without identity.

turns.text:
Revered Nāgasena, who takes rebirth?

What, is it this same mind-and-matter itself that takes rebirth?

If, revered sir, this mind-and-matter itself does not take rebirth would one not be freed from evil deeds?

Mind-and-matter, sire, takes rebirth.

This same mind-and-matter does not itself take rebirth, sire; but, sire, by means of this mind-and-matter one does a good or bad deed and, because of this deed, another mind-and-matter takes rebirth.

If, sire, it did not take rebirth one would be freed from evil deeds. But because, sire, it takes rebirth one is not freed from evil deeds. ... Suppose, sire, some man were to steal another man’s mangoes and the owner of the mangoes were to seize him and bring him before the king... and he were to say, ‘Your majesty, I did not steal his mangoes; the mangoes he planted were different from these that I stole; I do not deserve punishment.’ Would he, sire, not deserve punishment?

fields.intent: Uses a concrete legal case (theft) to expose the flaw in the King's moral loophole.

turns.text: Yes, revered sir, he would deserve punishment.
For what reason?

fields.intent: Forces the King to articulate the causal link himself.

turns.text: Whatever he may say, the mangoes he stole resulted from the mangoes which, he admits, the other man planted.
Even so, sire, by means of this mind-and-matter one does a good or bad deed and, because of this deed, another mind-and-matter takes rebirth; therefore, one is not freed from evil deeds.

fields.intent: Applies the legal logic (causal origin) back to the metaphysical problem.

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, is there such a thing as an experiencer?
What does this ‘experiencer’ mean, sire?

fields.intent: Asks the King to define the term 'experiencer' to set up the deconstruction.

turns.text: A soul within that sees a visible form with the eye, hears a sound with the ear... Just as we who are sitting here in the palace can look out of any window we want to look out of, even so, revered sir, this soul within can look out of any door it wants to look out of.

I will talk to you, sire, about the five doors. Listen and attend carefully. If the soul within sees a visible form through the eye just as we who are sitting here in the palace can look out of any window we want to look out of... can it not hear a sound, smell a smell, taste a taste, feel a touch and discriminate mental states through each of the other five doors besides the one you have specified in each case?

fields.intent: Tests the analogy: if the soul is free like a man in a room, why is it bound to specific senses for specific data?

turns.text: No, revered sir.

Again, sire, we who are sitting here in the palace will see visible forms out there before us more clearly in the great space if these network windows are removed. Thus too, would this soul within see visible forms more clearly when the doors of the eyes are removed? And if the ears were removed, the nose removed, the tongue removed, the body removed, would it hear a sound, smell a smell, taste a taste and feel a touch more clearly on account of the great space?

fields.intent: Pushes the analogy to absurdity: if the eyes are just windows blocking the view, removing them should improve vision.

turns.text: No, revered sir.
Because, sire, of the eye and visible form eye-consciousness arises. ... Thus these things are produced from a condition and there is no experiencer found here.

fields.intent: Replaces the Homunculus model with the model of dependent origination (eye + form -> consciousness).

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, where eye-consciousness arises, does mind-consciousness also arise there?
Yes, sire, mind-consciousness also arises there.

fields.intent: Establishes the basic premise of the system (co-arising) before explaining the mechanism.

turns.text: Now, revered sir, does eye-consciousness instruct mind-consciousness, saying ‘Where I arise do you likewise arise,’ or does mind-consciousness instruct eye-consciousness, saying ‘Where you arise I will likewise arise’?
No, sire, there is no conversation between them.

fields.intent: Rejects the student's projection of 'conversation' (intent) onto a mechanical process.

turns.text: Then how is it, revered Nāgasena, that where eye-consciousness arises there mind-consciousness also arises?
It is because of tendency, sire, because of door, because of habit and because of practice. ... When it is raining by what means may the water run away?

fields.intent: Introduces a physical analogy (rain/slope) to explain coordination without intention.

turns.text: It might run away by means of some slope.
But, sire, if it continued to rain, by what means would that later amount of water run away?

fields.intent: Extends the analogy to the 'following' behavior, paralleling the eye-to-mind sequence.

turns.text: It would take the same course as the earlier water.

Then, sire, does the earlier water instruct the later, saying ‘You run away by the same course as I do,’ or does the later water instruct the earlier, saying ‘I will also run away by the same course as you will take’?

fields.intent: Applying the 'instruction' theory to the water to show how absurd it sounds.

turns.text: No, revered sir, there is no conversation between them; they run away because there is a slope.
Even so, sire, it is because of tendency that where eye-consciousness arises, mind-consciousness arises there too.

fields.intent: Finalizes the structural model: Tendency acts like the slope, creating order without intent.

turns.text:
Revered Nāgasena, is it the case that one does not transmigrate and yet is reborn?

How, revered Nāgasena, is it that one does not transmigrate and yet is reborn? Make a simile.

Yes, sire, one does not transmigrate and yet is reborn.

Suppose, sire, some man were to light a lamp from another lamp. Did one lamp pass over to the other?

fields.intent: Uses the flame analogy to model transmission of pattern/energy without transmission of substance.

turns.text: No, revered sir.
In the same way, sire, one does not transmigrate and yet is reborn. ... Do you remember, sire, when you were a boy learning some verse from a teacher?

fields.intent: Reinforces the first analogy with a second, intellectual one (learning a verse) to make it personal to the King.

turns.text: Yes, revered sir.
But, sir, did that verse pass over from the teacher?

fields.intent: Clarifies that the teacher did not lose the verse when the student gained it (non-subtractive transmission).

turns.text: No, revered sir.
In the same way, sire, one does not transmigrate and yet is reborn.

fields.intent: Final confirmation of the doctrine using the established analogies.

turns.text:
Revered Nāgasena, for whom is the greater demerit: he who does an evil deed knowingly or he who does an evil deed unknowingly?

Well then, revered sir, do we doubly punish any of our family or our court who does an evil deed unknowingly?

He who took hold of it unknowingly, sire, would be more severely burnt.

His is the greater demerit, sire, who does an evil deed unknowingly.

What do you think about this, sire? If a man should unknowingly take hold of a red-hot ball of iron, glowing with heat, and another should take hold of it knowingly, which would be more severely burnt?

Even so, sire, the greater demerit is his who does an evil deed unknowingly.

fields.intent: Shifts from the legal domain (punishment) to the physical domain (burning) to prove the cost of ignorance.

turns.text:
Revered Nāgasena, does he who does not obtain Nibbāna know that Nibbāna is happiness.

But how, revered Nāgasena, does anyone without obtaining Nibbāna know that Nibbāna is happiness?

Yes, revered sir, they would know.

They know, revered sir, from having heard the lamentations of those whose hands and feet have been cut off that the cutting off of them is suffering.

Yes, sire, he does.

What do you think about this, sire? Would those who have not had their hands and feet cut off know that the cutting off of them is suffering?

How would they know?

In the same way, sire, anyone who has heard those who have seen Nibbāna knows that Nibbāna is happiness.

fields.intent: Completes the mapping: hearing lamentations (pain) is parallel to hearing teachings (bliss).

turns.text:
Revered Nāgasena, have you ever seen the Buddha?

Then have your teachers seen the Buddha?

Well then, revered Nāgasena, there is no Buddha; the Buddha is not manifested here.

Yes, revered sir; what doubt is there?

No, revered sir. ... But articles of use enjoyed by the former noble warriors are to be seen... By these we can know and can believe that the former noble warriors existed.

No, sire.

No, sire.

But, sire, did those former noble warriors exist who were the forerunners of your noble warrior dynasty?

Have you, sire, ever seen the former noble warriors?

Even so, sire... There are, sire, articles of use enjoyed by that Blessed One... that is to say, the four foundations of mindfulness... By these the world with the devas knows and believes that there was this Blessed One. ... As, sire, a city-architect... might build a city there... When that city was fully developed, he might go away to another district... When these people had seen the city, new, well laid out... they would know by inference: ‘Clever indeed is that city-architect who was the builder of the city.’

fields.intent: Completes the model: The Dhamma is the 'City' left behind, from which we infer the 'Architect' (Buddha).

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing mark of mindfulness?
Not-drifting, sire, is a distinguishing mark of mindfulness and also taking up is a distinguishing mark of mindfulness.

fields.intent: Provides a precise functional definition of mindfulness.

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, how is tranquillizing a distinguishing mark of faith? Make a simile

As, sire, the store-keeper of a Wheel-turning King reminds him of his glory every morning and evening, saying: ‘You have so many elephants, your majesty, so many horses... so much wealth; let his majesty remember it,’ and does not drift in regard to the king’s wealth. Even so, sire, when mindfulness is uprising one does not drift in regard to mental states that are wholesome and unwholesome...

fields.intent: Uses the 'Treasurer' analogy to model the inventory/reminder function of mindfulness.

turns.text: Revered sir, how is taking-up a distinguishing mark of mindfulness?

Sire, when mindfulness is uprising one examines the qualities of mental states... and thinking: ‘These mental states are beneficial, these mental states are detrimental’... the one who is devoted to mental training removes the detrimental mental states and takes up the beneficial mental states.

fields.intent: Clarifies the second function (taking up) as active selection/filtering.

turns.text: Make a simile.

As, sire, the adviser-treasurer of a Wheel-turning King knows what is beneficial and what is detrimental for the king and thinks: ‘These are beneficial for the king, these are detrimental’... and then removes what is detrimental and takes up what is beneficial... even so, sire, when mindfulness is uprising one examines the qualities of mental states... and takes up helpful mental states.

fields.intent: Reinforces the model with the 'Advisor' analogy to explain the discriminative function.

turns.text:
How is it, revered sir, that because of door mind-consciousness also arises where eye-consciousness arises?
Make a simile

A king’s border-town has strong ramparts and only one gateway.
If a man wanted to leave that town how would he do so?

fields.intent: Introduces the border-town analogy to explain structural causality without intent.

turns.text: Through that gateway, revered sir.
If another man wanted to leave that town how would he do so?

fields.intent: Extends the analogy to the 'following' behavior, paralleling the eye-to-mind sequence.

turns.text: In the same way as the first man, revered sir.

Then, sire, does the earlier water instruct the later, saying ‘You run away by the same course as I do,’ or does the later water instruct the earlier, saying ‘I will also run away by the same course as you will take’?

fields.intent: Applying the 'instruction' theory to the water to show how absurd it sounds.

turns.text: No, revered sir, there is no conversation between them; they run away because there is a slope.
Even so, sire, it is because of tendency that where eye-consciousness arises, mind-consciousness arises there too.

fields.intent: Finalizes the structural model: Tendency acts like the slope, creating order without intent.

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, is there the Buddha?
Yes, sire, there is the Blessed One.

fields.intent: Asserting existence to provoke the King's spatial assumption.

turns.text: But is it possible, revered Nāgasena, to point to the Buddha and say that he is either here or there?
Sire, the Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna... It is not possible to point to the Blessed One and say that he is either here or there.

fields.intent: Introduces the concept of Nibbana as cessation of location/being.

turns.text: Make a simile.

What do you think about this, sire?
When the flame of a great mass of fire has gone out, is it possible to point to that flame and say that it is either here or there?

fields.intent: Uses the extinguished fire analogy to model cessation.

turns.text: No, revered sir, that flame has ceased, it has vanished.

Even so, sire, the Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna... It is not possible to point to the Blessed One who has come to an end and say that he is either here or there.
But, sire, it is possible to point to the Blessed One by means of the body of the Dhamma, for Dhamma, sire, was taught by the Blessed One.

fields.intent: Completes the model: physical presence is gone (extinguished), but structural presence (Dhamma) remains.

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, is the body dear to those who have gone forth?
Sire, the body is not dear to those who have gone forth.

fields.intent: Asserting the ideal of detachment to provoke the King's charge of hypocrisy.

turns.text: Then why, revered sir, do you treasure and foster it?
But when you have gone into battle, sire, have you been wounded by an arrow from time to time?

fields.intent: Uses the King's own experience (battle) to introduce the concept of instrumental care.

turns.text: Yes, I have, revered sir.
Then, was not the wound anointed with ointment, smeared with oil and bandaged with a soft cloth?

fields.intent: Establishing the fact of care.

turns.text: Yes, revered sir, it was.
But was that wound dear to you, sire, that it was anointed with ointment, smeared with oil and bandaged with a soft cloth?

fields.intent: The core distinction: care does not equal attachment.

turns.text: That wound was not dear to me, revered sir, and it was only anointed with ointment... so that the flesh might heal.

Similarly, sire, the body is not dear to those who have gone forth;
but those who have gone forth and are without cleaving look after the body for the sake of faring the holy life.

fields.intent: Applies the wound logic to the body: the body is a tool (instrument) for the holy life, not an object of love.

turns.text: But those beings who are suffering painful... agonies in hell... can these poor, burning wretches be afraid of death?
Yes, they can.

fields.intent: Affirms the counter-intuitive fact (suffering beings fear the cure of death) to provoke inquiry.

turns.text:
But, revered Nāgasena... why should beings in hell be afraid of death which would release them from that certain pain?
... This I do not believe... They must rejoice at the prospect of the very condition they long for.

Death, sire, is a cause for fear for those who have not seen the Four Noble Truths... Suppose, sire, a boil were to arise, full of pus, on a man’s body, and he... wanting to escape from the danger of it, were to call in a surgeon... and the surgeon... were to have a lancet sharpened... Would not fright arise in that afflicted man, sire, with the cutting of the sharp lancet...?

fields.intent: Uses the surgery analogy to explain the conflict between fearing the process (pain) and desiring the result (cure).

turns.text: Yes, revered sir.
If the sick man who wants to be free from his ailment can be afraid of pain, just so can beings in hell, though they long to be released from it, be afraid of death.

fields.intent: Finalizes the resolution of the paradox: Instinct (fear) overrides Logic (desire for release).

turns.text:
Revered Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing mark of faith?

Revered Nāgasena, how is tranquillizing a distinguishing mark of faith? Make a simile.

Faith, sire, has tranquillizing as a distinguishing mark and also leaping forward as a distinguishing mark.

As, sire, a Wheel-turning King going along a high road with his four limbed-army... might cross a small stretch of water and, as a result, that water will become foul, turbid and muddy.
... The king might have a water-clearing gem. So the men cast that water-clearing gem in the water.
Immediately the various water plants disappear, the mud subsides and the water becomes clear, pure and serene.
... Sire, like the water is the mind... like the water-clearing gem is faith.
... Faith, as it is uprising, extirpates the hindrances...

fields.intent: Uses the 'Treasurer' analogy to model the inventory/reminder function of mindfulness.

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, this too was said by the Blessed One: ‘All beings tremble at punishment, all fear death.’ But again he said: ‘An arahat has passed beyond all fear.’ ... If the Blessed One said that all beings tremble at punishment... then the statement that the arahat has passed beyond all fear must be false.

Sire, it was not with regard to arahats that the Blessed One spoke... The arahat is an exception... Suppose, sire, a king had four chief ministers... and that when some business had arisen the king should have a command issued... ‘Let everyone pay me a tax’... Now, sire, would any tremor due to the fear of taxation arise in those four chief ministers?

fields.intent: Resolves the contradiction by introducing a hierarchical model where the general rule ('all fear') has specific exemptions.

turns.text: No, revered sir.
For what reason, sire?

fields.intent: Forces the King to articulate the logic of immunity.

turns.text:
Because the king has placed them in the highest positions, taxation does not affect them;
they are beyond taxation.
Even so, sire, the statement that all beings tremble at punishment, all fear death, does not apply to the arahats.

fields.intent: Finalizes the resolution: Arahats are structurally immune to the 'tax' of fear.

turns.text:
Revered Nāgasena, it was said by the Elder Sāriputta... ‘In the conduct of speech, the Tathāgata is quite pure.’ On the other hand... he addressed him with harsh words, calling him a foolish fellow.
... Now if the first statement is correct, the allegation that the Tathāgata called the Elder Sudinna a foolish fellow must be false.

What the Elder Sāriputta said is true... But that was not said out of rudeness of disposition... If any man, sire, in this birth, does not understand the Four Noble Truths... he is called a foolish fellow. Therefore, the Blessed One addressed the Elder Sudinna with words of truth...

fields.intent: Reframes the 'harshness' as factual accuracy, challenging the social definition of politeness.

turns.text: But, revered Nāgasena, if someone should abuse another, even though he speaks the truth, we would inflict a small fine on him.
Have you, sire, ever heard of anyone bowing down before... a wrong-doer?

fields.intent: Uses the King's own social logic (respect/disrespect) to show that 'abuse' is sometimes appropriate status recognition.

turns.text: No, revered sir...
Well then, sire, did the Blessed One act properly or not?

fields.intent: Forces the King to concede the propriety of the act based on the previous admission.

turns.text: Properly, revered Nāgasena.
Now, sire, would a physician administer pleasant things as medicine in a case where all the humours of the body were affected...?

fields.intent: Reframes the 'harshness' as medical necessity (instrumental pain for cure).

turns.text: No, revered sir, wishing to put an end to the disease he would give sharp and scarifying drugs.

Even so, sire, the Tathāgata gives instructions for the allayment of all the diseases of the defilements.
... As, sire, hot water softens anything that can be softened... even so, sire, the Tathāgata’s words, even when harsh, are full of benefit...

fields.intent: Finalizes the model: Harshness is a tool for softening/healing, not an expression of anger.

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, this too was said by the Blessed One: ‘I am without wrath...’ On the other hand, the Tathāgata dismissed the Elders Sāriputta and Moggallāna... did the Tathāgata dismiss the company when he was angry or did he dismiss it when he was pleased?
Sire... that was not through ill-temper. Suppose, sire, some man stumbled over a root... Would it be that the great earth, angry with him, made him fall?

fields.intent: Reframes the dismissal as an impersonal reaction (like gravity) rather than an emotional one (anger).

turns.text:
No, revered sir.
The great earth feels neither anger against any man nor delight.

Even so, sire, there is no ill-temper or satisfaction in the Tathāgatas.
... As to this, sire, the great ocean does not endure association with a corpse.
... Now, sire, is the great ocean angry that it casts up that corpse?

fields.intent: Strengthens the 'impersonal system' model with the Ocean analogy (active rejection without emotion).

turns.text: No, revered sir... the great ocean is free from approval and repugnance.

Even so, sire... So the company was dismissed on account of what it itself had done through its own fault.
... But though the Tathāgata, sire, dismissed those monks, he desired their welfare...

fields.intent: Finalizes the model: systemic rejection (mechanism) is compatible with desire for welfare (intent).

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, this too was said by the Blessed One: ‘A monk should not attempt suicide...’ But on the other hand you say: ‘On whatsoever subject the Blessed One was addressing the disciples, he always... taught the Dhamma in order to bring about the destruction of birth...’

The regulation you quote, sire, was laid down by the Blessed One, and yet our saying you refer to is true.
There is a reason for this...

fields.intent: Validates the paradox as real but resolvable.

turns.text: What, revered Nāgasena, may that reason be?

One who is moral, sire, possessed of morality, is like an antidote... like a healing balm... like a ship... It was in order that one who was moral like that might not perish... that the Blessed One... laid down this rule of training...

fields.intent: Reframes life not as an intrinsic good to be clung to, nor an evil to be destroyed, but as a resource (ship/antidote) for others.

turns.text:
Revered Nāgasena, these givers, when they bestow their offerings, devote (the merits) specifically to former relatives... Now do the dead derive any benefit from them?

But if the offerings made by such givers benefit certain of the departed... then if a man who destroys living creatures... were to dedicate it to the departed... would it then be transferred to them?

Some do, sire, and some do not.
... The fourth class that lives on the gifts of others do derive benefit...

No, sire.

fields.intent: Flatly denies the student's logical extension (that evil transfers like good) to set up the distinction.

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, what is the cause, what is the reason that a good deed can accrue to them and not an evil one?

An evil deed is slight, sire, a good deed is abundant.
... Make a simile. ... It is as, sire, one small drop of water might fall on the earth, yet would that drop of water, sire, spread out over ten or twelve leagues?

fields.intent: Explains the non-transfer of evil via the 'Drop' analogy (lack of volume/magnitude).

turns.text: No, revered sir...

Even so, sire, an evil deed is slight... it affects only the doer... But as, sire, a mighty and great cloud were to pour down rain satisfying the earth’s surface, yet would the water from that great cloud, spread out all round?

fields.intent: Uses the 'Cloud' analogy to explain why good (merit) spreads and can be shared.

turns.text: Certainly, revered sir.

Even so, sire, a good deed is abundant;
because of its abundance one is able to share it even with devas and mankind.

fields.intent: Finalizes the doctrine: merit transfer depends on the 'abundance' property of the deed.

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, is there a spot to the east or the south... where Nibbāna is stored up?
There is no spot, sire... where Nibbāna is stored up.

fields.intent: Denies the spatial premise of the King's question.

turns.text: If, revered Nāgasena, there is no place for the storing up of Nibbāna, well then, there is no Nibbāna... As there are... fields producing crops... mines producing gems... even so, revered Nāgasena, if there is Nibbāna, there must be a place for producing Nibbāna.

fields.intent: Uses the friction/fire analogy to explain how something can exist as a potentiality without a physical storage depot.

turns.text:
Revered Nāgasena, this Dispensation... is mighty... It is not right to let a layman go forth so long as he is a mere householder.
... Because of their backsliding people may think: ‘Vain, indeed, must be this Dispensation... that these people have turned back from it.’

Supposing, sire, there were a pond full of pure, clear, cold water.
Some man, dirty... should come there, and without bathing in it should turn back again, still dirty as before.
Whom would the people blame... the dirty man or the pond?

fields.intent: Uses the 'Pond' analogy to shift the locus of failure from the System (Dispensation) to the User (Backslider).

turns.text: The people would blame the dirty man... What defect is there in the pond?

Even so, sire, the Tathāgata constructed the pond of the noble true Dhamma... Or, sire, it is as if a man afflicted with a dire disease should visit a physician... but he does not let himself be treated and turns back still an ill man.
Whom would the people blame...?

fields.intent: Reinforces the point with a second analogy (Doctor/Patient) to make the user error undeniable.

turns.text: The people would blame the sick man... What defect is there in the physician?

Even so, sire... Or, sire, it is as if a famished man arriving at a mighty distribution of food... but not eating any of that food, should turn back famished as before, whom would the people blame...?

fields.intent: Third analogy (Food/Famished Man) to overwhelm any remaining resistance to the argument.

turns.text: The people would blame the famished man...
Even so, sire... If someone, not partaking of that meal, turns back... the people would blame only him...

fields.intent: Finalizes the argument: The System (Dhamma) is perfect; the failure lies entirely with the User who does not engage.

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, it has been said by the Blessed One: ‘Ānanda, the true Dhamma will last now for only five hundred years.’ But, on the other hand... ‘If these monks were to live rightly, the world might not be empty of arahats.’ If the first of these statements is correct, the second is misleading...

The Blessed One, sire, did make both statements... The one deals with the duration of the Dispensation, the other illustrates the practice... Suppose, sire, there is a reservoir full of fresh clean water... If the water in that reservoir had not dried up and a great cloud above should pour down heavy and continuous rain, would the water in that reservoir be exhausted and dried up?

fields.intent: Resolves the time-limit paradox by introducing a dynamic system model (Reservoir + Rain).

turns.text: No, revered sir.

Even so, sire... If the sons of the Buddha were to make the rain of the cloud of good behaviour... pour down heavily... so would this reservoir... last for a very long time... If, sire, people were to continually polish with fine soft red powder a stainless mirror... would dirt and dust and mud arise on its surface?

fields.intent: Links the 'Rain' element to 'Practice', showing how human agency extends the system's life.

turns.text:
No, revered sir.
On the contrary, it would become even more stainless than before.
Even so, sire... Grounded on practice, sire, is the Dispensation of the Teacher... It will last so long as practice does not disappear.

fields.intent: Finalizes the model: The Dispensation's duration is conditional on continuous practice (maintenance).

turns.text: Revered Nāgasena, this too was said by the Blessed One... ‘When I am gone, Ānanda, let the Order, if it should so desire, abolish the lesser and minor rules of training.’ Now, revered Nāgasena, were these lesser and minor rules of training wrongly laid down... since the Blessed One allowed them to be abolished...?

In both cases, sire, the Blessed One said as you have declared.
But in the second case it was to test the monks that he said it... As, sire, a king of kings might say to his sons: ‘This great country... reaches to the sea... It is hard to maintain it much longer with the forces we have... So, my children, when I am gone, you had better abandon the outlying districts...’ Now, sire, would the princes... give up those outlying districts...?

fields.intent: Reframes the permission to abolish rules as a 'loyalty test' using a political analogy.

turns.text:
No, revered sir, kings are greedier than that.
The princes... would never give up what they already possessed.

Even so, sire, the Tathāgata spoke thus testing the monks... Sire, the sons of the Buddha... would preserve even more than another hundred and fifty rules of training-how then should they let go of the rules of training that had been laid down originally?

fields.intent: Finalizes the reframe: The monks' refusal to abolish rules proves their zeal, validating the test.

turns.text: I was meditating deeply.

Why are you so lazy? The bell rang long ago.

If meditation makes you deaf, it is not meditation.

fields.intent: Destroys the student's spiritual excuse by defining true meditation as including awareness.

turns.text: What is Buddha?
The mind that asks is already wrong.

fields.intent: Invalidates the question itself by pointing to the conceptual mind as the error.

turns.text: Then what should I do?
KATZ!

fields.intent: Uses a sudden shout to cut off the student's conceptual searching entirely.

turns.text: Master, why do we chant for the dead if nothing is born or dies?
If *you* die, will chanting help?

fields.intent: Shifts from abstract doctrine to immediate personal reality to expose ignorance.

turns.text: I... don't know.
Correct.

fields.intent: Validates the admission of 'don't know' as the correct state.

turns.text: If everything is empty, why can't I drink wine?
Is this palm empty?

fields.intent: Sets up a concrete test of the student's abstract understanding of 'emptiness'.

turns.text: Yes.

*slaps palm loudly*

If you still feel the emptiness, drink all the wine you want.

fields.intent: Uses immediate physical sensation to contradict the intellectual claim of emptiness.

turns.text:
A mouse ate the cat’s food and the bowl broke.
What does it mean?
If you open your mouth, you are wrong.

fields.intent: Blocks the usual channel of explanation (speech).

turns.text: If you close your mouth, you are wrong.

fields.intent: Closes the trap: neither speech nor silence is allowed, forcing a jump to a higher level.

turns.text:
Master, the mouse ate the cat’s food and the bowl broke.
What does it mean?
If you answer, wrong.

fields.intent: Blocking the student from answering intellectually.

turns.text: Then I won’t answer.
If you don’t answer, wrong.

fields.intent: Blocking the student from retreating into silence.

turns.text: Then what should I do?
See before thinking.

fields.intent: Directing the student to immediate perception before conceptualization arises.

turns.text: It is on the diagonal, Socrates.
Yes, certainly.
From what has been said, can we now say that the square of double area is formed on the diagonal of the original?
It appears, Socrates, that it is as you say.
We must therefore take heart and not accept that idle argument of yours, for it would make us lazy; instead we must be eager to search out what we do not know.
I do not understand, Socrates, what you mean by saying that true opinion is not less useful than knowledge.
Yes, it seems so to me now.

True opinions, as long as they stay in place, are a fine thing and do all the good that knowledge does, but they are not willing to stay for long; they must be tied down by an account of the reason why. This tying down is recollection, and when they are tied, they become knowledge. You might compare them to the statues of Daedalus: if they are not tied down, they run away; if they are tied, they stay.
Then are we to say, Socrates, that virtue comes to those who possess it not by teaching but by some other way?

If there are no teachers of virtue, it is not by knowledge that virtuous men are virtuous. It looks rather as if true opinion guides them, like a gift from the gods, until they are tied down by an account—if they ever are. We have not found what virtue itself is, but we must not give up searching for it.

Callias, If your two sons had been born colts or calves, we would have been able to get and hire an overseer for them who could make the two of them noble and good in their appropriate virtue, and he would have been someone from among those skilled with horses or skilled in farming. But as it is, since they are two human beings, whom do you have in mind to get as an overseer for the two of them? Who is knowledgeable in such virtue, that of human being and citizen? For I suppose you have considered it, since you possess sons. Is there someone, or not?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Quite so,
turns.speaker: CALLIAS

turns.text: Who, and where is he from, and for how much does he teach?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Evenus, Socrates, from Paros: five minae.
turns.speaker: CALLIAS

turns.text: Now come here, Meletus, tell me: do you not regard it as most important how the youth will be the best possible?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: I do.
turns.speaker: MELETUS

turns.text: Come now, tell these men, who makes them better? For it is clear that you know, since you care, at least. For since you have discovered the one who corrupts them, as you say, namely me, you are bringing me before these men and accusing me. But the one who makes them better—come, tell them and reveal to them who it is. Do you see, Meletus, that you are silent and have nothing to say? And yet does it not seem to be shameful to you, and a sufficient proof of just what I say, that you have never cared? But tell, my good man, who makes them better?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: The laws.
turns.speaker: MELETUS

turns.text: But I am not asking this, best of men, but rather what human being is it who knows first of all this very thing, the laws?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: These men, Socrates, the judges.
turns.speaker: MELETUS

turns.text: What are you saying, Meletus? Are these men here able to educate the young, and do they make them better?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Very much so.
turns.speaker: MELETUS

turns.text: All of them, or some of them, and some not?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: All of them.
turns.speaker: MELETUS

turns.text: Well said, by Hera, and you speak of a great abundance of benefiters. What then? Do the listeners here make them better or not?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: These too.
turns.speaker: MELETUS

turns.text: And what about the Councilmen?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: The Councilmen too.
turns.speaker: MELETUS

turns.text: Well, Meletus, then surely those in the Assembly, the Assemblymen, do not corrupt the youth? Or do all those too make them better?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Those too.
turns.speaker: MELETUS

turns.text: Then all the Athenians, as it appears, make them noble and good except me, and I alone corrupt them. Is this what you are saying?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: I do say this, most vehemently.
turns.speaker: MELETUS

turns.text: You have charged me with great misfortune. Now answer me. Does it seem to you to be so also concerning horses? That all human beings make them better, while one certain one is the corrupter? Or is it wholly opposite to this, that one certain one is able to make them better—or very few, those skilled with horses—while the many, if they ever associate with horses and use them, corrupt them? Is this not so, Meletus, both concerning horses, and all the other animals?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Of course it is, altogether so, whether you and Anytus deny or affirm it. For it would be a great happiness for the young if one alone corrupts them, while the others benefit them. But in fact, Meletus, you have sufficiently displayed that you never yet gave an thought to the young.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: But tell us further, Meletus, before Zeus, whether it is better to dwell among upright citizens or villainous ones? Sir, answer. For surely I am asking nothing hard. Do not the villainous do something bad to whoever are nearest to them, while the good do something good?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Quite so.
turns.speaker: MELETUS

turns.text: Is there anyone, then, who wishes to be harmed by those he associates with, rather than to be benefited? Keep answering, my good man. For the law orders you to answer. Is there anyone who wishes to be harmed?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Of course not.
turns.speaker: MELETUS

turns.text: Come then, do you bring me in here saying that I voluntarily corrupt the young and make them more villainous, or involuntarily?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Voluntarily, I say.
turns.speaker: MELETUS

turns.text: What then, Meletus? Are you so much wiser at your age than I at mine, that you have become cognizant that the bad always do something bad to those who are closest to them, and the good do something good; whereas I have come into so much ignorance that I am not even cognizant that if I ever do something wretched to any of my associates, I will risk getting back something bad from him? So that I do so much bad voluntarily, as you assert? Of this I am not convinced by you, Meletus, nor, do I suppose, is any other human being. But either I do not corrupt, or if I do corrupt, I do it involuntarily, so in both cases what you say is false.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Is there any human being, Meletus, who believes that there are human matters, but does not believe in human beings?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Is there anyone who does not believe in horses, but believes in horse-matters? Or anyone who does not believe in flute-players, but believes in flute-matters? There is not, best of men... But at least answer what comes next. Is there anyone who believes that there are daimonic matters, but does not believe in daimons?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: There is not.
turns.speaker: MELETUS

turns.text: How helpful you were by answering reluctantly when compelled by these men! Now then, you say that I believe in and teach daimonia; so whether they are novel or ancient, at any rate I do believe in daimonia according to your speech... But if I believe in daimonia, then surely there is also a great necessity that I believe in daimons. Is this not so?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: And do we not believe that daimons are either gods or children of gods? Do you affirm this or not?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Quite so.
turns.speaker: MELETUS

turns.text: Therefore if I do believe in daimons, as you say, and if, on the one hand, daimons are gods of some sort, then this would be what I say you are riddling and jesting about, when you say that I do not believe in gods, and again that I believe in gods, since in fact I do believe in daimons. On the other hand, if daimons are certain bastard children of gods... then what human being would believe that there are children of gods, but not gods?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: The Pythia replied that no one was wiser.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: When I heard these things, I pondered them like this: "What ever is the god saying, and what riddle is he posing? For I am conscious that I am not at all wise, either much or little. So what ever is he saying when he claims that I am wisest? Surely he is not saying something false, at least; for that is not sanctioned for him."
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: I went to one of those reputed to be wise... and when I considered him and conversed with him... it seemed to me that this man seemed to be wise, both to many other human beings and most of all to himself, but that he was not.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: For my part, as I went away, I reasoned with regard to myself: "I am wiser than this human being. For probably neither of us knows anything noble and good, but he supposes he knows something when he does not know, while I, just as I do not know, do not even suppose that I do. I am likely to be a little bit wiser than he in this very thing: that whatever I do not know, I do not even suppose I know."
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: After the politicians I went to the poets... So I would take up those poems of theirs which it seemed to me they had worked on the most, and I would ask them thoroughly what they meant, so that I might also learn something from them at the same time.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Almost everyone present, so to speak, would have spoken better than the poets did about the poetry that they themselves had made. So again, also concerning the poets, I soon recognized that they do not make what they make by wisdom, but by some sort of nature and while inspired... At the same time, I perceived that they supposed, on account of their poetry, that they were the wisest of human beings also in the other things, in which they were not.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Finally, then, I went to the manual artisans... And I was not played false about this: they did have knowledge of things which I did not have knowledge of, and in this way they were wiser than I.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: But, men of Athens, the good craftsmen also seemed to me to go wrong in the same way as the poets: because he performed his art nobly, each one deemed himself wisest also in the other things, the greatest things—and this discordant note of theirs seemed to hide that wisdom.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: So I asked myself on behalf of the oracle whether I would prefer to be as I am, being in no way wise in their wisdom or ignorant in their ignorance, or to have both things that they have. I answered myself and the oracle that it profits me to be just as I am.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: If you would say to me with regard to this, "Socrates, for now we will not obey Anytus; we will let you go, but on this condition: that you no longer spend time in this investigation or philosophize; and if you are caught still doing this, you will die—"
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: If you would let me go, then, as I said, on these conditions, I would say to you, "I, men of Athens, salute you and love you, but I will obey the god rather than you; and as long as I breathe and am able to, I will certainly not stop philosophizing, and I will exhort you and explain this to whomever of you I happen to meet..."
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: "Are you not ashamed that you care for having as much money as possible, and reputation, and honor, but that you neither care for nor give thought to prudence, and truth, and how your soul will be the best possible?"
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: With a view to these things, men of Athens, either obey Anytus or not, and either let me go or not, since I would not do otherwise, not even if I were going to die many times.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: What, then, am I worthy to suffer or to pay because I did not keep quiet during my life...?
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Something good, men of Athens, at least if you give me what I deserve according to my worth in truth—and besides, a good of a sort that would be fitting for me.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: What, then, is fitting for a poor man, a benefactor, who needs to have leisure to exhort you? There is nothing more fitting, men of Athens, than for such a man to be given his meals in the Prytaneum, much more so than if any of you has won a victory at Olympia with a horse or a two— or four-horse chariot.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: For he makes you seem to be happy, while I make you be so; and he is not in need of sustenance, while I am in need of it. So if I must propose what I am worthy of in accordance with the just, I propose this: to given my meals in the Prytaneum.
turns.speaker: SOCRATES

turns.text: Socrates, you asked what piety is. I still say it is what I am doing now. Is this not sufficient?
I would be of no use, Socrates, if I did not have accurate knowledge of all such matters.
It certainly is.
The pious is what I am doing now: prosecuting a wrongdoer.
Very well, Socrates, I will try again: what is beloved by the gods is pious, and what is not beloved by them is impious.
Yes, we were.
It seems so.
I'm afraid so.
Explain again, Socrates — how must we examine this definition?
I don’t know what you mean.
Necessarily.
Socrates, whatever I put forward keeps wandering off and will not stay where we put it.
They would stay put for me, at least; you are the one who makes them move.
Piety is the part of justice that is attending to the gods.
By Zeus, no.
The kind slaves provide to masters.
Saying and doing what is pleasing to the gods in prayers and sacrifices.
Some other time, Socrates. I am in a hurry and must go.
But by Zeus, Euthyphro, do you think you have such accurate knowledge about piety and impiety that you are not afraid of committing another impiety by prosecuting your father?
Then teach me. Isn’t the pious always the same as itself, and the impious the opposite of the pious?
So tell me what the pious itself is.
I asked for the form itself, not an example of one of the many pious things.
Weren’t we just saying that the gods disagree with one another?
Then the same things will be loved by some gods and hated by others.
So the same act would be both pious and impious?
Consider: is the pious loved by the gods because it is pious, or is it pious because it is loved?
We say something is carried because it is being carried, not the reverse. Likewise something is loved because it is being loved.
Then the pious is loved because it is pious — not pious because it is loved.
These things seem to belong to my ancestor Dedalos — your definitions do not stay put.
Then I must be more skilled than Dedalos, moving not only my arguments but others’. Yet I want them fixed more than wealth.
Does attending mean benefiting them, as horse-training benefits horses?
Then what kind of attending is it?
And what is the great work the gods accomplish using us as servants?
So the pious is what is pleasing to the gods — again?
We must begin again from the beginning to examine what the pious is — I will not give up until I understand it.
To suffer it. No one would choose the other.
Of course—everyone admits that.
Yes, that seems to follow.
How can punishment benefit the one who suffers it?
You’re saying the criminal is made better by suffering?
How can that be? He gets whatever he wants.
You’re saying the tyrant—the freest man—is actually the worst off?
That’s a ridiculous image, Socrates.
I deny that such a life is miserable.
Yes. I stand by that.
It can be.
No—that’s absurd.
Yes, he does—if he is to be an orator at all.
Certainly. That is part of his craft.
I am trying, Socrates, but you keep shifting the topic.
Very well, ask again.
Yes—the greatest of human powers.
Not necessarily. But that doesn't lessen his power!
By nature, Socrates, the stronger and better should rule the weaker.
The one, of course—the superior man.
That’s not what I meant.
The life of the man who indulges his desires freely.
Because pleasure is the good.
Of course not. I exercise discipline like any man of sense.
Yes, but that doesn’t mean one should practice it constantly.
Yes, because his craft demands it.
You’re smuggling your assumptions into my view.
I won’t answer your childish questions anymore.
I’m tired of your traps.
Fine—ask again.
That’s just myth-making.
And what truth is that supposed to reveal?
You boast that, yet the city ignores you.
And what is it you want from me, then?
Polus agreed with you that doing what’s unjust is more shameful than suffering it. As a result of this admission he was bound and gagged by you in the discussion, too ashamed to say what he thought.
Yes. He was forced to contradict himself because he dared not say what he truly believed.
Socrates, you’re grandstanding in these speeches, acting like a crowd pleaser.
You twist everything—first forcing Gorgias to contradict himself, and now Polus.
Yet here you are persuading—using rhetoric to deny rhetoric.
Still, you must use the very craft you condemn to defend your view.
Doing it.
Suffering it is worse.
I don’t know what you mean. Ask somebody else.
And I couldn’t care less about anything you say.
If an orator and a doctor competed before a city, the doctor would make no showing at all, but the orator would be appointed.
Such is the accomplishment of this craft.
Which do you think is worse, Polus—to do what’s unjust or to suffer it?
So you agree that doing injustice is shameful?
And what is shameful is bad, isn’t it?
Then doing injustice is worse than suffering it.
Being punished is the way the soul is relieved of its injustice.
Because punishment is a kind of cure, Polus. No one wants to keep the soul diseased.
Exactly—just as the sick body is better for painful treatment.
The man who does what’s unjust is miserable, Polus.
No—the one who does injustice and escapes punishment is the most miserable of all.
Yes. For he corrupts the soul most deeply and has no one to heal him.
The man devoted to unchecked pleasure is like a jar full of holes—no matter how much he pours in, it leaks out again.
Yet it’s your way of life I’m describing, Callicles—endless craving, never satisfaction.
But you agree the one who can be satisfied is better off than one who constantly needs refilling?
Do you say that the pleasant and the good are the same, Callicles?
Is it pleasant to scratch an itch endlessly?
Then the man covered in itching sores is living the best life, if he scratches constantly?
Then the pleasant and the good are not the same.
Tell me, Gorgias, does the orator know what is just and what is unjust?
And does he teach these things to others?
Then an unjust orator would not exist, for he knows justice and teaches it?
Please answer the question I put to you, Gorgias—shortly.
Not at all. You’re giving long speeches instead of the simple answer required.
I already did. You owe me the answer—not another speech.
You claim the orator has great power, Polus?
Does he know what is truly good and what is bad?
Then you’ve admitted he acts without knowledge—and the man without knowledge harms himself the most.
And you call ‘stronger’ the majority or the one?
Then if the many restrain this one by law, the many are stronger?
But it’s what you said—and your principle collapses under its own definition.
Tell me plainly, Callicles—what life are you defending as best?
And is this life admirable because it is pleasant, or for some other reason?
Then you must defend that principle to its end. Are you prepared to?
Tell me, Callicles—do you yourself indulge your desires without restraint?
Yet you said the best life is the unrestrained one.
Then you admit your doctrine contradicts your own way of living.
A pilot does not merely steer whichever way he wishes. He knows what is best for the ship and those aboard.
Then a man who rules must know what is best—not merely act on desire.
No—I’m showing that true power requires knowledge, just as navigation requires skill.
If you refuse to answer, there’s no way for us to examine the truth together.
They are not traps, Callicles. They are conditions for any rational inquiry.
Fine—ask again.
Picture the soul, Callicles, stripped naked before the judge—every deed visible.
Myths teach truths the arrogant cannot hear plainly.
That injustice deforms the soul—and punishment restores it.
I am the only one of the Athenians, Callicles, who tries to practice the true political art.
Better ignored while doing right than praised while corrupting my soul.
Only this: choose which life you will live—the life of discipline or the life of ruin.
So you admit that shame compelled him—not understanding?
Then Polus conceded not conviction, but fear of appearing base before the many.
Either refute philosophy, or else, by the Dog, Callicles will not agree with Callicles, but will be out of harmony with himself all his life long.
It is better for the many to contradict me than for me to contradict myself, though I am only one person.
I already did. You owe me the answer—not another speech.
I believe I practice the true political craft, because my speeches do not aim at gratification but at what is best.
If I persuade, it is not as a pastry chef persuades children, but as a doctor speaking bitter truths.
I already did. You owe me the answer—not another speech.
Which do you think is more shameful, doing what’s unjust or suffering it?
And which is worse?
Then shame does not track evil—your claim collapses.
Isn’t disciplining the soul better for it than indulgence?
This fellow won’t put up with being benefited and disciplined.
I already did. You owe me the answer—not another speech.
So persuasion defeats knowledge among the ignorant.
And such is why it must be used justly, lest it mislead those who lack expertise.
As far as forming a judgement about what is written and spoken.
turns.speaker: Interlocutor

turns.text: As far as judging about melody.
turns.speaker: Interlocutor

turns.text: By no means.
turns.speaker: Interlocutor

turns.text: What faculty then will tell you?
turns.speaker: Interlocutor

turns.text: And what is this faculty?
turns.speaker: Interlocutor

turns.text: How far does the grammatic art possess the contemplating power?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: And how far music?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Does either of them then contemplate itself?
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: But when you must write something to your friend, grammar will tell you what words you must write; but whether you should write or not, grammar will not tell you. And so it is with music as to musical sounds; but whether you should sing at the present time and play on the lute, or do neither, music will not tell you.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: That which contemplates both itself and all other things.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: The rational faculty; for this is the only faculty that we have received which examines itself, what it is, and what power it has, and what is the value of this gift, and examines all other faculties...
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: If, then, you ask me whether you should hold the chamber pot or not
But this would not be worthy of me.
For to one man it is consistent with reason to hold a chamber pot for another... But to another man not only does the holding of a chamber pot appear intolerable...
I shall say to you that the receiving of food is worth more than the not receiving of it... so that if you measure your interests by these things, go and hold the chamber pot.
Well, then, it is you who must introduce this consideration into the inquiry, not I; for it is you who know yourself, how much you are worth to yourself...
But convince me of this that you acted naturally, and I will convince you that everything which takes place according to nature takes place rightly.
I do not deny that: but the matter about which we are inquiring is whether such behavior is right.
I cannot; but do you rather show me how it is not according to nature and is not rightly done.
The sight.
I do not know.
The greatest harm.

For in respect to this matter we must say that tumours also come for the good of the body, because they do come; and generally we must say that to do wrong is natural, because nearly all or at least most of us do wrong. Do you show me then how your behavior is natural.
Well, if we were inquiring about white and black, what criterion should we employ for distinguishing between them?
Well then, since we are inquiring about things which are according to nature, and those which are done rightly or not rightly, what kind of criterion do you think that we should employ?

And yet not to know the criterion of colors and smells, and also of tastes, is perhaps no great harm; but if a man do not know the criterion of good and bad, and of things according to nature and contrary to nature, does this seem to you a small harm?
Well then?
Why then do you tell me to make myself like the many?
Because you consider yourself to be only one thread of those which are in the tunic.
It was fitting for you to take care how you should be like the rest of men... But I wish to be purple, that small part which is bright, and makes all the rest appear graceful and beautiful.
And if I do, how shall I still be purple?
What matter is this?
turns.speaker: Interlocutor

turns.text: When I see a man anxious, I say, "What does this man want? If he did not want something which is not in his power, how could he be anxious?" For this reason a lute player when he is singing by himself has no anxiety, but when he enters the theatre, he is anxious... for he not only wishes to sing well, but also to obtain applause: but this is not in his power.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: He knows not what a crowd is or what the praise of a crowd is. However he has learned to strike the lowest chord and the highest; but what the praise of the many is... he neither knows nor has he thought about it. Hence he must of necessity tremble and grow pale.
turns.speaker: Epictetus

turns.text: Man, what are you talking about? Me in chains? You may fetter my leg, but my will not even Zeus himself can overpower.
